Mr. Speaker, I now learn that the quotation is from the agreement between Canada and the United States of America to govern the establishment of a distant early warning system in Canadian territory, which was effected by an exchange of notes with Washington on May 5 of this year, 1955. There were certain additional words not included in the-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: That is it.
In the quotation in the Tribune.

speechtext: That is why I did not agree.

The way the sentence actually read was as follows:
All contact with Eskimos other than those whose employment on any aspect of the project is approved is to be avoided, except in cases of emergency.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and Naiional Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition raised
a question concerning restrictions that have been placed upon contacts with the Eskimos by men engaged in the construction and operation of the distant early warning line. He referred particularly to a report in the New York Herald Tribune of Sunday, May 29, attributed to Mr. Gerald Waring of the press gallery, which he quoted as saying that all contact with the Eskimos is to be avoided except in cases of emergency. I said yesterday I did not think I could agree with the quotation because according to my memory there was more to it than that. The Leader of the Opposition at the opening of the sitting agreed with me that the quotation was not complete.
Yesterday I dealt briefly with some of the considerations in this matter, and I undertook to take the question as notice and prepare a more detailed statement for today. With regard to my answer to this question the Leader of the Opposition said, as reported on page 4219 of Hansard of May 30:
In preparing his reply I hope that it may be one which will explain what does appear to many writers in the United States to be a rather unusual restriction upon the ordinary friendly contacts of members of the United States forces who are in Canada.
Again this afternoon the Leader of the Opposition referred to this aspect of the question.
I wish to say first of all that the regulations in question are not directed at the United States forces only. They are directed at any and all people having to do with the D.E.W. line. Everybody knows that the eastern portion of that line is being built by a Canadian contractor, the Foundation Company of Canada, Limited. The western part is being built by Northern Construction Company Limited, which is also a Canadian contractor.
However, I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that the restrictions which have been placed upon contacts may not be fully understood by many people in the United States. Might I draw his attention to the article to which he referred, in which we find a number of reasons why this agreement has been entered into. May I quote just two short extracts:
"The Eskimos are in a primitive state of social development", the Canadian government said in its note to the state department. "It is important that these people be not subjected unduly to disruption of their hunting economy, exposure to diseases against which their immunity is often low, or other effects of the presence of white men which might be injurious to them.

D.E.W. Radar Line
As a matter of fact that is practically what I said yesterday. Another quotation:
The government, which has a large scale program under way to broaden the base of the Eskimo economy and combat disease, is faced with medical evidence that the natives have little natural resistance to even relatively innocuous diseases of civilization.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, it must be remembered that in the area from Coppermine eastward the Eskimos have had very little contact with our way of life. They are not used to our ways or customs. They do not understand what money is or what wage employment is.
As to the character of the restrictions, I might point out that they do not go so far as the New York Herald Tribune suggested, that is to exclude "all contact... except in cases of emergency." The provision is that employment should be under terms and arrangements concurred in by the department of northern affairs, and that other contact is to be avoided except in cases of emergency.
Might I just add that by coincidence this matter was under discussion yesterday by a standing committee on Eskimo affairs at the very moment the Leader of the Opposition inquired concerning it. This is an advisory committee consisting of the deputy minister and officials of the department of northern affairs; the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; Bishop Marsh, the Anglican bishop of the Arctic; Bishop Tro-cellier, who is in charge of the Roman Catholic diocese of Mackenzie and who was yesterday represented by Father Laviolette of the Catholic Indian educational services; Mr. Chesshire, general manager of the fur department of the Hudson's Bay Company, and officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare. The committee, I am told, spent more than three hours on Eskimo problems arising out of the distant early warning line. They considered particularly the provisions with regard to employment and contact, and the representatives of both churches, of the Hudson's Bay Company and of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and the other government officials were in complete agreement as to the necessity for the restrictions and with their character and application.

Mr. Speaker, I would point out that my question yesterday was directed to the articles I had seen, and I mentioned particularly one which quoted directly from the Canada-United States agreement. I would point out that the opening part of the section
[Mr. Lesage.l
of the agreement which deals with Canadian Eskimos has this to say;
It is important that these people be not subjected unduly to disruption of their hunting economy, exposure to diseases against which their immunity is often low, or other effects of the presence of white men which might be injurious to them.
If we have reached the point, Mr. Speaker, when we have to put an iron curtain around our own white men in our own country-
Oh, oh.

-then there is indeed a problem with which we are called upon to deal. We have been proceeding for these past few years and, in fact, for generations, in the belief that the contact of the white man with primitive races in different parts of the world was to the advantage of those peoples. If in fact these requirements are necessary, then there is something to be done with regard to the white people just as much as with regard to the Eskimos.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think I can allow that statement to go without reply. I believe the policy of the government and the department is sound. It has been approved by people who have had a great deal of experience with the Eskimo population. If the Leader of the Opposition wishes to substitute his own judgment for that of all the advisers whom I have consulted, and is satisfied to do that, that is up to him.
Mr. Speaker-
Order.

-on a question of privilege, there was no introduction of my judgment into this matter. I was simply raising the point that these regulations impose restrictions regarding the association of white men with people who are described as a primitive race; and if this is to be the attitude of the government it is a strange attitude indeed, having regard to the extent to which we are trying to advance the interests of primitive races in every part of the world by contact with white men.
Mr. Speaker, as between the Eskimos and some white men, I would choose the Eskimos.
I agree with you.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. Will the minister report briefly to the house on his visit last week to the fire-ravaged areas of Nova Scotia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Halifax for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question.
Severe forest fires swept through several areas of Nova Scotia a week ago and centred particularly in the Mount Uniacke, Timberlea, St. Margarets Bay, Bridgewater and Liverpool areas. At that time the damage to buildings was reported to be particularly heavy in the latter two regions. Some of the fires raged uncontrolled for several days. During this period we were in constant touch with the premier of Nova Scotia, local municipal officials and others, and learned that in addition to considerable woodland, about 80 buildings and some livestock were destroyed in Lunenburg and Queens counties. Fortunately no lives were lost.
On Friday last, thanks to my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney), I flew over the devastated areas in a Royal Canadian Navy helicopter and subsequently visited on the ground. I took the opportunity of extending to those who sustained losses the sympathy of the government and of the people of Canada generally. Some of the people to whom I spoke had lost the results of a lifetime of hard work. I also met with the relief committees.

What struck me most forcibly, in addition to the losses, were the heroic efforts of fire fighters who, through extraordinarily hard work, were able to keep the property loss from being vastly greater than it was, and the magnificent manner in which the people of the stricken areas have rallied to the support of those who have suffered. The Salvation Army, the Red Cross and radio station CKBW in particular have done outstandingly good work. Officials of the departments of fisheries and public works were in the fishing centres to render what assistance they could.
Campaigns are now under way to raise funds to re-establish those who have suffered losses, and particularly to provide fishermen and farmers with the tools of production so they can soon again produce and earn. The relief committees are working diligently at collecting funds and assisting where necessary in caring for those who have lost their homes. The response has been good, but more money is needed and the appeal is continuing.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, May 30, consideration in committee of Bill No. 410, to amend the Customs Act-Mr. McCann-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On section 1-Duty to report.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last night I suggested that while section 18 of the Customs Act, having stood on the statute books for a long time, may now be in need of revision, in my opinion the legislation now before us has taken a very extreme form. I should like to ask the minister if, on further reflection, he has concluded that the legislation should take a less extreme form, and that it is not fair to place upon every person arriving in Canada, on foot or otherwise, the statutory duty to proceed to the nearest customs house regardless of whether it is near or far?
Does the minister think it proper that before a person travelling in a vehicle terminates his journey he should have to proceed to that customs house and there give to the officer in charge an inventory of all goods in his charge or custody? I am sure all members of the house want to see all the teeth put in this legislation that are reasonably required, but it is going a long way to put a statutory duty on everyone who enters Canada at any place-a place, for instance, which might be 25 miles from the nearest customs house-to proceed to that customs house before he may stop or go home or do anything else.
Customs Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Before the minister answers the question, may I say something apropos of what the hon. member for Eglinton has said. Representing a border riding, naturally I am very anxious, as are other people along the border, about this clause in the bill. We are wondering, and I think it has come about through erroneous reports, whether or not everyone crossing the bridges will be forced to enter the customs yard and subject themselves to a thorough investigation by the customs officers.
Last year at the port of Niagara Falls alone we had 1,100,000 cars of both the permit and non-permit class, and at the Fort Erie port there were some 1,400,000 cars in these two classes. Many of these people have asked me, especially people from Buffalo who own summer places along the lake shore, if they would be required to go into the customs yard every time they crossed the border. I should like to point out to the minister that I am not a lawyer, for which I am very thankful, but a reading of the section would lead one to believe that every commuter or non-commuter will be obliged to enter the customs yard and subject himself to a thorough examination by the customs officer every time he crosses the border.
Up until a few years ago there was a shortage of officers on the United States side of the Peace bridge to examine the cars desiring to enter the United States. I have seen cars lined up for two miles because of the shortage of officers. If this bill means what I think it must, and what I hope it does not, it would cause not only a traffic hazard but a great deal of inconvenience to the commuters. I would be greatly relieved, and I believe the customs officers would be as well, if the minister would make a statement verifying the fact that there will be no change in procedure. Certainly the customs officers are the ambassadors of friendship, and are the first people our tourists meet. In view of the millions of dollars the tourists leave annually in Canada I believe we should do everything we can to ease their way into this great dominion. I hope the minister will give me some clarification of this bill so I can explain to the people what it actually means.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
To set the minds of the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Niagara Falls at rest, I will say that there is no change, and no change is contemplated, in the procedure which has been followed for the last 40 or 50 years. I have crossed a lot of borders myself in Europe, and I know of no country where one would not have to report upon entering the country. There has

Customs Act
been no change whatever in that. We are putting it into the law here, but the commuters will not suffer any inconvenience whatever.
As a rule what happens is that the first time one enters the country, say from Buffalo over to Fort Erie, he is given a sticker to put on his car. This sticker identifies him as he comes along and the customs and immigration officials at that point know the person and see that he is not held up for one minute.
We felt that at this time we should put it into law, and the purpose of the amendment is to require all vehicles arriving in Canada to report to customs in order to ensure the proper administration not only of the Customs Act but of all other acts which are enforced by customs officials. This includes, as I said yesterday, acts and regulations relating to immigration, health, the health of animals and so on. I do not believe this ought to call for much controversy. It is a practice of many years' standing that is being regularized now by law.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I find the minister very difficult to follow. The hon. member for Eglin-ton and the hon. member for Niagara Falls have pointed out the practical considerations. The hon. member for Eglinton pointed out that if we read this literally it seems to involve people, for instance, in the western country where there are many rural roads, in almost impossible inconvenience. When the minister says nothing is going to be altered, does he mean that in the situation so clearly described last night by the hon. member for Eglinton the people are just going to disregard the law?
After all, when the minister says there is going to be no change that means either one of two things. Either we are not reading this correctly, and I think that is not the case, or it is not going to be followed through. Let the minister take the case described by the hon. member for Eglinton last night and describe what happens and how this may be within the four corners of this section. I cannot see how it could be. Last night the hon. member for Eglinton described the case of a man coming across the border perhaps 20 miles from the nearest officer or reporting station, and outlined the possibility, if this section means what it seems to mean, of this man having a duty to take that journey of 20 miles there and 20 miles back before he has discharged his duty to the customs authorities. Now the minister says this is not going to change anything. If it is not going to change anything then this seems to me to mean nothing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
This section under discussion reads as follows:
Every person in charge of a vehicle arriving in Canada, other than a railway carriage, and every person arriving in Canada on foot or otherwise, shall
(b) before unloading or in any manner disposing thereof, make a report in writing to the collector or proper officer at such custom-house-
I believe this has been the practice at every customs port in Canada as far back as I can remember. I fail to see any change there. I have some knowledge of water transportation and transportation by vehicle, and within my memory there has never been a time when the practice outlined in paragraph (b) has not been applied.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: Read paragraph (a).

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: I have read it, and I cannot see anything in (a) that would change the customs procedure in this country from what it has been for as far back as I can remember.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Charlotte is quite right. I want to read section 20 (1) in the Immigration Act:
Every person, including Canadian citizens and persons with Canadian domicile, seeking to come into Canada shall first appear before an immigration officer at a port of entry or at such other place as may be designated by an immigration officer in charge, for examination as to whether he is or is not admissible to Canada or is a person who may come into Canada as of right.
We believe the same principle ought to apply with reference to customs ports. I doubt very much if there are any places, in any event not many places, where one would be so inconvenienced that he would have to travel 40 miles, as the hon. member for Eglinton suggests, to report to an office. The offices at which a person could report are much closer together than that. A man coming into Canada, no matter in what kind of vehicle, knows he has to report so does not go the long way around. He does not go along two sides of the triangle when he could go by a direct route that would bring him to a port where he could declare any goods he may have and at the same time declare to the immigration officers that he is entering Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister's earlier remarks were intended to be reassuring, but unfortunately his remarks seem to be at variance with the explanatory note in the bill. The explanatory note, after quoting the provisions of the present section 18, goes on to say:
The purpose of the amendment is to require all persons to report.

I daresay if, as the minister says, there is to be no change in the method of enforcement, no change in procedure at the border, if it were accepted, that would allay some of the apprehension of hon. members in the face of the very extreme language of the new section. However, we then have the explanatory note which seems to be in keeping with the plain provisions of the new section, that the purpose of the amendment is to require all persons to report.
It is one thing to say there is no change contemplated in the procedure at the border. The hon. member for Niagara Falls, who lives closely with this problem, will want very definite assurance that it is not a matter left simply to the whim of the local customs officer. Here we are not dealing with language which says that any person entering Canada shall report if called upon to do so by a customs officer. This new section purports to lay upon him a duty to report, and it is not one that is enforceable simply at the whim of the officers.
I am still greatly troubled by the case I have put, where a man enters Canada by a route that is not close to one of the border points in common use, and which is not close to a customs house. If the minister is going to put a statutory duty on that man then there are going to be a great many unwitting law-breakers in this country, in the face of language that seems to me to be very extreme.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is a legal requirement. I am afraid the hon. member thinks that if a man comes over the border into Canada he must immediately go to the customs office and declare. If it happens in the middle of the night and the nearest port is closed, we accept that man's entry at the earliest possible convenience for him, which would be the next day. So there is no inconvenience there. It is a legal requirement, and I think the hon. member for Niagara Falls will testify to the fact that this has worked out well both at Niagara Falls and at Fort Erie, two of the largest customs centres from the point of view of the number of people entering Canada.
We have had practically no complaint with reference to this requirement. As I say, it has been going on for years and years, and the change is that now it is put in the law. It was the law that if they had dutiable goods they must go and declare them. If this measure passes it will be the law that, whether or not they have dutiable goods, as early as is practicable and possible they will have to go to the nearest customs office and declare whether or not they have anything
Customs Act
that is dutiable. They must do that anyway for immigration purposes. Therefore no extra inconvenience is thrown on them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the position were as the minister has stated it we would not need to spend much time discussing it, because that would be reasonable. But unfortunately what the minister has said is not what is said by the language of the section. The minister has said that certain things can be done "as early as is practicable". He cites the case of the customs house being closed in the middle of the night. If it said "as early as practicable" that would be the saving provision; it would be the sensible thing and would take some of the sting out of the clause as I find it.
Unfortunately, however, the minister's interpretation of what the clause means is not what the clause says. Let us look at section 18 (b), which says:
Every person in charge of a vehicle arriving in Canada, other than a railway carriage, and every person arriving in Canada on foot or otherwise, shall . . .
(b) before unloading or in any manner disposing thereof, make a report in writing to the collector or proper officer at such custom-house or station of all goods in his charge or custody or in the vehicle and of the fittings, furnishings, and appurtenances of the vehicle-*
And so on. There is no language there that says he is to do it as soon as is practicable. And there is nothing in paragraph (a) that says that when a customs house is closed it will be sufficient if he comes back and makes his report as soon as possible. On the contrary, the language of (a), the language of (b) and of (c) are all mandatory and unqualified. Let us look at 18 (a) which says, in effect, that if a person arrives in Canada he shall go to the customs house nearest to the point at which he arrived in Canada.
It is all very well when he is going to a customs house at a border point, where such customs house is located right at the point where he enters Canada. But there are many places where people enter Canada today where there are no customs houses located near the point where they are setting foot on Canadian soil.
I suggest the minister should look at the language and trim it down until it meets what he has said is the purpose of the legislation. He has pointed out that the person is to do what is practicable in the circumstances, and if that language were inserted it would meet the objections, the fears and the apprehensions in the minds of hon. members about the section as it stands. Mr. Chairman, I have not had an opportunity to look up the latest agreement between the contracting parties on tariffs and trade, but it seems to me that in this clause there is a violation of the Geneva agreement. This reads:
Wherever duty ad valorem is imposed on goods imported into Canada, the value for duty shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of this section.
Then it spells out the various methods of appraising articles for duty purposes. Then subsection 6 reads:
When the value for duty cannot be determined under the preceding subsections for the reason that
(a)	like or similar goods are not sold for use or consumption in the country of export, or
(b)	there is no established market in the country of export for like or similar goods,
the value for duty of the goods shall be such value as the minister determines.
My understanding of the Geneva agreement on tariffs and trade is that we agreed that no valuation would be made on an arbitrary or fictitious basis. If that is so, then it seems to me this provision proposed by the minister conflicts directly with

that agreement to which we, in common with the other contracting parties who are signatories, agreed. My contention is that this provision should be rejected by the committee or withdrawn by the minister because it gives the minister the right to establish a fictitious value, an arbitrary value, which is not permitted under the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
It seems to me that those of us who are interested in a tariff policy which does not allow arbitrary valuations which may lead a country into the establishment of prohibitive tariffs on certain types of goods entering the country cannot accept this provision. With its avowed philosophy of freer trade, fairer trade and lower tariffs I believe that if the government look at this provision they will agree that it should not be in the bill. It is quite incompatible with what the government profess in regard to tariffs and so on.
There are countries where goods are produced for export which are not used in the country of manufacture. We can think of a country where the climate is not sufficiently severe to encourage people to wear mitts or gloves, but those articles may be manufactured in that country for export to Canada. Under this provision the fair market value in the country of origin would not be the determining factor, nor would the value of like goods if you could find goods there of that description. The minister is to have the arbitrary power to fix the value for duty purposes without regard to the internal or domestic prices of the country of origin.
I suggest to the minister that he should not press this clause this afternoon, but that he take another good look at it and also at the general agreement on tariffs and trade. I have not had an opportunity to look up the particular clause to which I have referred, but I think my memory is correct that the Geneva agreement absolutely prohibits a contracting country establishing arbitrary values on goods that may be imported into such country. I ask the minister to take another look at this clause before he presses for its passage.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer a question of the hon. member for Greenwood with reference to dumping duty collected in the following calendar years. In 1950 it was $1,735,543; in 1951, in round figures, $1,547,000; in 1952, $1,373,000; in 1953, $1,102,000; and in 1954-this is preliminary, as the accurate figures are not available- $1,114,000.
It might perhaps serve the purpose if I deal with these different sections and give the explanation for them. Subsection 2 is the section which states the primary rule for establishing value for duty, and in no way changes the present provisions which provide for valuation for duty purposes of imported goods at home market prices in the country of export.
Subsection 3 is new. It is intended to provide a basis for value for certain classes of importations not covered by the general provisions of subsection 2. It also seeks to remove from the present law a very serious difficulty arising in such instances from the almost unworkable rule of determining the "nearest ascertainable equivalent" to what is in effect a non-existing home market value.
This kind of problem arises where a sale is made to Canadian importers under special conditions for which there is no comparable marketing situation in the country of export. Most typical of these cases would be where the special conditions of sale result from the Canadian importer dealing with a related foreign company in a trade relationship which does not exist between the exporter and any other parties in the country of export. That is a new condition of business that has arisen in this country within the past few years.

We come now to subsection 4. It merely carries forward a portion of the present subsection 1. It is applied where value cannot be established under the previous subsections and permits the appraisal of goods in such instances to be based on the home market value, at which goods similar to those imported are sold for home consumption to various classes of trade in the country of export comparable to the trade status of the importer in Canada and in quantities comparable to those imported.
We come now to subsection 5, which is a new provision. It provides for cases where the importation, not having been capable of valuation under the preceding sections, requires more specific provisions. This subsection covers cases where the goods exported to Canada are not identical with but are similar to goods sold in the country of export, and which are sold to Canada under special conditions which have no comparable counterpart in the home market structure. This subsection, as in subsection 3, provides for valuation at the home market value at which the similar goods are sold to the trade in the country of export.
Subsection 6 is also new, and is the one about which I believe the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was inquiring. It again is applied only when the previous sections offer no basis for valuation. The kind of case for which this subsection is designed is where appraisal cannot be made because of peculiar marketing methods in the country of export such as, for instance, where goods are not sold with transfer of property rights but only leased. Shoe machinery and International business machines are instances of that.
Subsection 7 in essence brings forward the present subsection 3, which provides for cases where appraisal cannot be made under any of the valuation provisions based on home fair market values. It is somewhat similar to the preceding section and is invoked when the former does not apply; for instance, where semi-processed goods are imported for further processing in Canada-that relates to a great many parts for cars-but are never sold in that condition in the country of export. In the country of origin they are finished, but they are shipped to Canada perhaps as castings and then they are burnished here and further fitted. One has to make an appraisal for duty purposes of those.
Subsection 8 is a repetition of a provision now in the present section 1. There is no change in substance. The principle of value for duty in no case to be less than the selling
Customs Act
price to the importer in Canada is continued. In common practice the value is never less than the selling price.
Subsection 9 makes it clear that internal taxes to be disregarded for valuation for duty shall be taxes imposed directly upon the goods in the country of export, and not assessments upon producers, or upon wages for social security of various kinds, income taxes, etc. This condition obtains with reference to goods manufactured in and exported from France. These duties are added to the value. The general provision for the disregarding of such taxes is at the present time contained in subsection 4, which has not been found to be sufficiently specific.
Subsection 10 is the same as the old subsection 5. As to subsection 11, this amendment will authorize a segregation of the value of goods from the value of services where the price of the imported article combines both charges. There are numerous examples, one being, for instance, the importation of unassembled educational kits, the cost of which includes the value of a course. Of course you could not put a value on the course, but when there is an educational kit accompanying it that is appraised and the duty is applied to it. Another example would be a person who might go from Fort Erie to Buffalo to consult a doctor. The doctor will charge a fee and probably will prescribe medicine or treatment of some kind. You do not pay duty on the doctor's knowledge. You pay it on the article brought into the country, whether it be medicine or an appliance. The same thing obtains with reference to architectural and engineering plans. They are often brought into the country. We do not assess duty on the value of the knowledge, experience and scientific equipment that went into their preparation. We put a value on the plans themselves for duty purposes.
I think that explains pretty well all the subsections of the new section 35. I do not know that there is anything more I can add, but I shall attempt to answer any further questions that may be asked with reference to it.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to avail myself of the privilege that this motion

affords to place before the house a positive motion for the consideration of hon. members. There are occasions when members on the government side are inclined to ask in a rather complaining way why the opposition does not put forward positive and constructive proposals. I submit that the record will show that many positive and constructive proposals have been made.
Nevertheless it is the function of the opposition acting as it does in the capacity of auditor, in so far as that is permitted, to examine the business that is done and to criticize where criticism seems appropriate. A motion of this kind provides the mechanism for seeking the favourable consideration of something which seems to be to the advantage of the house as representatives of the people of Canada. What I propose to place before the house now I suggest is something calling for the earnest consideration of every member of this house and of everyone in Canada at this time.
Profound changes have taken place in the life of our people and in the Canadian economy within the past few years. We have seen industrial enterprises expand beyond recognition and individual activities extend to a much wider field. However, in no single activity within our country has there been a wider and more rapid expansion than in the field of government itself. Much of that was imposed by the dreadful demands of war; much of it was imposed by the necessity for improvising when sudden new requirements called for the setting up of organizations or agencies which had not previously existed. However, there is this great difference.
I do not believe that there is a single business of any size in this country which has expanded greatly within recent years which has not deemed it advisable to examine thoroughly its expanded structure and to seek outside independent advice as to how that greatly expanded structure can be guaranteed and brought into an efficient integrated entity to the best advantage of all those working with it and of all those who depend upon its success. Any business enterprises which have not done that already are doing it now and there is a very important reason therefor.
The post-war sellers' market is gone and new competitive conditions are arising everywhere throughout the world. Within our domestic markets as well as in foreign markets we are feeling the direct impact of the highly competitive atmosphere in which business is now being conducted. The adjustment required to meet those conditions is something that is going to spell success or failure, advancement or disaster within those years immediately ahead.
Government Services
We are telling ourselves constantly that the nation's business is the largest business of all, and I submit that the time is long overdue for Canadians generally and for the representatives of all Canadians in particular who sit here in this house to examine the position and to take those steps that are appropriate to bring the largest business in Canada into a position of efficiency as every businessman would do if he were confronted with the same circumstances.
I am not suggesting for one moment that at this time, when we see so much evidence of the effects of this highly competitive world market upon our own export trade and upon our domestic business, the adjustments needed to meet this situation can be made by governments alone, but certainly if there is one place where an example can be given and where the action taken can be of advantage to everyone meeting a situation of this kind, it is in the case of the government itself. If the organization of government and all its agencies were to be examined in the same objective manner as any successful business has already been examined, then there would be, not only an enormous saving of public funds, but an encouragement to people generally to prepare themselves in the most effective way for the very competitive period through which we are going to pass. The action of the government in this respect could be decisive in determining the attitude of our people. It is not only because of the competitive market that this should be done; it should also be examined because of the impact of inflation upon hundreds of thousands of our people.
Do not let anybody repeat again in this house that we have avoided inflation in Canada. We have had very heavy inflation. Our dollar today is worth considerably less than half of the pre-war dollar in purchasing power. Those who are able to work with their hands and to combine the efforts of their hands with the skill of their brains in the great competitive activities, those who are engaged in the professions, those who are in business, have been able to adjust their position and actually in many cases to take some advantage of inflation itself. Let us examine, however, what this has meant to hundreds of thousands of people dependent upon the small income from their life savings, to all those thousands who are dependent upon railway pensions, upon military pensions, upon pensions from insurance companies or endowment policies of various kinds. Think of what this means for everyone on a small income. Think of what it means in cases you actually know of people who worked hard, performed great service and looked forward to declining years, not

Government Services
in comfort but with an adequate amount to give them that measure of happiness and security that they had a reason to expect when they looked at the number of dollars that would be coming in. There is no one in this house who does not know someone today, who does not know several people, who are finding it, not difficult, but impossible to make ends meet because of the effect of inflation.
In the midst of great plenty, in the midst of very evident prosperity, there is in fact great hardship in this country at this time. Now, the cruel results of inflation are something which we should consider, because there is no single influence which does as much to create inflation as excessive government expenditure. That is not only because excessive government expenditure adds to the tax burden of our people and in turn adds to the cost of the things everyone buys; it is also a fact that where there is excessive government expenditure the ordinary standards which establish the cost of many products and many services are upset by the loose methods of handling these affairs by government agencies. Unless there is the same test in regard to the value of services and the cost of things that are bought in the case of a government agency as would apply in the case of a private agency, then you are creating the most vigorous inflationary force which can operate in any country.
For that reason, the first and most effective place to tackle inflation-and in tackling inflation to increase our ability to meet the competitive period in which we now are-is within the realm of government itself, the nation's business. The lengthening shadow of government in this country now extends over 25 per cent of the expenditure of all moneys in Canada. A quarter of what is spent in this country is spent by all the governments, federal, provincial and municipal. Seventy-seven per cent of that is spent by the government of Canada. Therefore, the place where the most effective job can be done in creating greater efficiency and reducing the inflationary pressures at this time is right here within this House of Commons to which, I hope, the government of Canada is still answerable.
In tackling any problem of this kind the essential consideration is to obtain the facts. We have not the facts today. That is not because an effort has not been made to obtain them. The facts cannot be obtained. The facts are hidden behind the front of those doors which contain the records that are not open to the members of this house through any mechanism now available to

us. Wherever any door has been opened- and I repeat this without any exception, wherever any door has been opened-it has been found that savings could be made by more efficient methods and by better bookkeeping and better organization. It is the duty of the members of this house to see that the facts are obtained. A thorough analysis of the administrative efficiency of government and of all the departments and agencies of government is long overdue. Careful and detailed analysis is required, because of the impact of all these activities upon all the business operations and the whole life of our people in this country.
Surely the figures that will impress this upon us most forcefully are the figures which indicate the tremendous increase in government expenditure within the short period of 15 years. For the year 1938-39, the last year before the war, the total amount spent by the government of Canada was $533,063,000. For the year 1954-55 the expenditure by this government was $4,255,387,000. This government is now spending eight times what the government was spending in the year before the war. No explanation related to increase in population, increase in national income, increase in productive capacity or any other explanation will give us the full story of those figures.
Eight times what the government spent in the last fiscal year before the war is now being spent. Yes, I realize that part of that figure is represented by money being turned over to the provincial governments, but that is only a fraction of this large figure. Surely any ordinary business seeing an expansion of eight times in its spending would say: Where can we do something about this? The government says: What would you suggest should be examined? Let us look at a few of the things that any ordinary business enterprise would examine very carefully. For instance, let us take the Department of National Defence, the Department of Defence Production, and civil defence, which can be bracketed together. Let us see what they spend.
I am not talking now about their expenditures for arms, for the men to perform the military duties, or expenditures to produce weapons and military requirements generally. Let us look at some of the figures that I know any business would examine if it were involved in spending such a huge amount of money. These figures only relate to those departments having to do with defence. May I ask hon. members to listen to them and remember that this is well within the time that a number of members now in the house have been sitting here.

First of all let us take travel and removal expenses. In the year before the war-and in every case where I use that expression it will refer to the fiscal year 1938-39-they amounted to $1,101,000. The amount in the estimates for this year is $46,084,300-$1,101,-
000	before the war and $46,084,000 fifteen years later.
Let us look next at the expenditures for telephones, telegrams and other communication services. There is not a businessman who does not know that in any business where anybody can grab a telephone and make long distance calls you can throw more money away within a short space of time than perhaps in any other single way. They have very careful ways of checking the propensity of the ordinary person to listen to a distant voice and to exchange ideas by telephone when it could be done just as well by a letter which would be carried there by airmail in 24 hours or 48 at the outside, with good service. Listen to these figures for telephones, telegrams and other communication services, and remember that they relate only to defence activities. In the last year before the war the amount was $57,000, not an insignificant figure. This year the estimate is $6,843,150. You know, you cannot help wondering whether something could not be done to encourage the use of letters with airmail delivery by way of substitution for some of these calls. In fact, every hon. member of the house knows perfectly well that unless there is an objective examination of figures of that kind by outside experts nobody here will begin to know the nature of the calls that have multiplied these expenditures so enormously.
Then, let us talk about publicity and the various things that go with it, again just for defence. In the year before the war the amount spent was $5,000. There must have been certain Scotch instincts operative at that time so far as publicity was concerned. The estimate for this year is $2,507,500. Then
1	come to office stationery, supplies, equipment and furnishings. In the year before the war the amount was $233,000. It will be recalled that there was a large reserve force at that time and also not comparable permanent forces but permanent forces with various headquarters staffs and so on. The amount then was $233,000 and the estimate for this year is $7,018,684. You can buy a lot of office furniture for $7,018,684.
Then we have another item not covered by publicity, namely, publication of departmental reports and other material. That is a nice euphonious name for some of the informative material that does not forget to give an apple to teacher at the same time. In

the year before the war nothing was spent on that item, but the amount in the estimates for the current year is $2,311,650. I have brought the items relating to defence together so that we shall not have anyone saying: Oh well, defence has made us spend this money.
Let me deal with the non-defence departments, and I am not dealing here with any of those things that can be regarded as fixed or rigid expenditures. Let us get back to travel and removal expenses for the nondefence departments, in this case not people urgently called upon to carry out some very dramatic duty. In the year before the war travel and removal expenditures amounted to $3,504,000. The amount this year is $15,770,736. Is there no room for examination there, Mr. Speaker? Is there no room for that question we saw printed on signs in the railway stations of Great Britain during the war-Is your trip really necessary? I think there could be some examination of these expenditures.
Let us look at telephones, telegrams and other communication services. In the year before the war the amount was $689,000, quite a substantial figure. You can do a lot of telephoning and sending of telegrams for that amount of money even if you have airmail service which was not available in the same way at that time. But let us see what the amount is now, even though we have an airmail service that transports letters right across the country so quickly. Instead of $689,000 the amount for this year is $7,356,469.
Then there is publicity, and oh, how publicity-conscious this government is! In the last year before the war the amount was $1,794,000 for the non-defence departments, and this year the amount is $7,663,790. That of course does not include any of the host of people who have been attached to the various staffs to make sure that their own people are not forgotten.
Then we have the publication of departmental reports and other material. There again, strangely enough, before the war not a cent was spent on that, but this year $4,484,645 will be spent, quite a tidy sum to get out these reports on the habits of bees and birds, the mating activities of lobsters and things of that kind. I am not suggesting they all fall into that category but nevertheless we have seen some material which could only be described by a term that would be unparliamentary and which goes into the wastebaskets of most people who have any occupation for their time. It is certainly included in that figure of $4,484,645.

the second reading of Bill No. 408, to incorporate Trans-Border Pipeline Company Ltd.
Could we have an explanation of this bill?

The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to incorporate a pipeline company under the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act. As hon. members know, before any company can engage in the operation of a pipeline which crosses a provincial or international border, it must be incorporated by an act of parliament pursuant to the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act. Of course, the matter is subsequently referred to the board of transport commissioners.
This bill follows the usual pattern of pipeline bills which come before this house. Probably the important clause is clause 5, which I will read:
The company shall have all the powers, privileges and immunities conferred by. and be subject to all the limitations, liabilities and provisions of the Pipe Lines Act, and any other general legislation relating to pipelines enacted by parliament with respect to the transportation of gas and oil and other liquid and gaseous hydrocarbons.
Now, the purpose of the incorporators, if this legislation is enacted, is to acquire through lease or purchase a pipeline which was constructed during wartime and was known as the Canol project. This pipeline is one in existence now between Skagway in Alaska and Whitehorse, Yukon Territory. As I say, this pipeline was constructed during wartime by the United States authorities with the con-

sent of the Canadian government to receive petroleum products which were brought in by tanker to Skagway. At that point these products were discharged into storage facilities and then transported by pipeline for the use of the army and air forces.
I am informed that the United States authorities are now constructing or have constructed a new 8-inch line from Haines, Alaska, to a point on the Alaska highway. The old pipeline was a 4-inch line. It is likely that this 4-inch pipeline between Skagway, Alaska, and Whitehorse in the Yukon Territory will no longer be required by the United States authorities and will, therefore, be available for lease or purchase. The proposed company is prepared to acquire this pipeline.
It may be of interest to note that Yukon Pipelines Limited, the bill incorporating which was recently before this house, apparently has the same idea in mind and seeks to acquire the same line. I feel that a little competition is always beneficial. Should this bill be given second reading, Mr. Speaker, I intend to have it referred to the proper standing committee where more detailed information will be given.

There is one feature of this bill that I should like to bring out, and that is that while the purpose of the applicants is to compete with the White Pass and Yukon railway the bill which the officials of that railway got through this house contains a proviso which has not been written into the bill now before the house. When the Yukon Pipelines Limited bill came up for second reading it was sponsored by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). At that time he explained that he proposed to ask in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines that there be a proviso written into the bill to the following effect:
Provided that the main pipeline or main pipelines for the transmission of gas and gaseous hydrocarbons shall be located entirely within Canada.
Now, that amendment was passed by the standing committee, and it has since been passed by the house. The Yukon Pipelines Limited bill now contains that proviso, subject of course to approval by the Senate. I do suggest to the sponsor of this bill that his bill should be subject to the same proviso. As a matter of fact, that proviso has been written into all the pipeline bills that have come before the house at this session. It was even written into the charter of Trans-Prairie Pipelines, Ltd., when their bill was before the standing committee.
I have seen no reason why Trans-Border Pipeline Company Ltd. should have any
Trans-Border Pipeline Company Ltd. advantage over the others. As a matter of fact the present applicants are proposing to try to get a pipeline which, I believe, is on the right of way of the White Pass and Yukon route. This pipeline was laid during the war by Americans, but now they are not using it. They are putting in a new line of their own which runs from Haines; and this pipeline along the right of way of the White Pass and Yukon route has to be taken over by someone.

Mr. Speaker, when the proceedings were suspended at five o'clock to consider private and public bills I was dealing with comparative expenditures as between the year before the war and the current year, and I shall continue to discuss that matter now.
I had mentioned the figures in regard to the publication of departmental reports and other material which, in the year before the war, had called for no expenditure, but which in the current year called for an expenditure of $4,484,645. Now, Mr. Speaker, these figures would suggest to anyone who has any sense of business responsibility that there should be an examination to see what can be done to increase efficiency, to improve the services and to co-ordinate some of those activities which have sprung up so rapidly under the pressures of war and the immediate post-war period. There is one way that this can be done, and that is for the government to set up an appropriate board of inquiry under the public Inquiries Act, with full power to examine this subject and to report to the government in the usual way. Radio Canada building, Montreal, represents a [DOT]capital investment of approximately $4,500,000. It is regarded as public property acquired for the international shortwave broadcasting service, but a substantial portion is occupied by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for purposes associated with its national service. The rental rate therefore is insufficient (a) to provide for depreciation, (b) to give a reasonable return on the capital investment, and (c) to recoup the cost of specially installed facilities. That is simply one of the findings, which indicates a reason for examining this whole general situation.
Then we have the letter of Mr. Watson Sellar, the Auditor General, to the Hon. James J. McCann, dated Ottawa, August 5,	1954.
Surely that letter would suggest to any businessman dealing with a similar proposition reasons why he should engage outside assistance to examine in a detached and objective manner the general organization of government and its agencies. The letter reads as follows:
Sir,
Re: Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
Having completed the audit of the accounts of the above-noted corporation for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, I now report to you, in compliance with the requirements of section 87 of the Financial Administration Act the results of the examination both of the accounts, and of the financial statement forwarded herewith.
Allowance for depreciation and obsolescence. The letter then finishes with the statement that subject to the foregoing it is found that the general accounts represent the situation. Any businessman responsible for the administration of a large business who found that the head of one of his departments was continuing to refuse to make changes necessary for the efficient supervision of the business of that department would act, and act very positively and quickly. It must be remembered that this is the largest business in Canada. I suggest that what should be done in regard to other types of business certainly should be done in this particular case.
Other governments have not shown themselves to be unwilling to admit that there can be changes and that there can be improvements. The fact is that other governments have been able to carry out very important improvements. I am reminded of the fact that in Great Britain they have examined a number of their departments under inquiries similar to that which I am proposing.
But, after all, we have one government very close to us, it is true under a different constitutional system but actually dealing with similar problems and having the experience of an almost parallel expansion of activities. While the constitutional structure is different, the general business activities of Canada and the United States are so similar that when we see the tremendous expansion such as we have seen in both Canada and the United States during the same years we can well examine what is done in both countries.
Therefore we are interested in finding that in the United States the government did not suggest that everything was perfect. They decided that it would be wise to act like businessmen when dealing with the largest business that there is. The hon. member seems to be suffering from some indescribable indisposition. The fact is that I know Ear falls very well. I opened the Ear falls plant, so I should know something about it. I know exactly what area it serves.
I am simply mentioning this to remind hon. members that there have been other inquiries which produced helpful results. I recall particularly the Hoover commission in the United States. The inquiries carried on by that commission were most successful and many changes that could be made were suggested.
In so far as the Hoover commission is concerned, I need not remind hon. members that that has been discussed before in this house. The United States government found that their first activities in this field were must successful so they then set up another commission with even wider powers. In doing so they have had the advantage of a team of experts who have been able to inquire into every aspect of government, including the production and distribution of power and things of that kind. They have obtained facts upon which a general discussion of this subject can take place.
As far as this particular activity is concerned, we might well recall that such an able administrator as General Eisenhower saw fit to renew the activities of the Hoover commission. The second Hoover commission was set up with what was described as a task force of 100 experts including widely experienced accountants, businessmen and
Government Services
others whose training would best qualify them to conduct an inquiry of this kind.
They have been inquiring into various aspects of government. One thing that they have been emphasizing is that under the tremendous impact of the improvised expansion which was necessary-I want to emphasize the words "was necessary"-during the war years a lack of integration in accounting methods and supervision resulted in methods that did not provide either the most efficient operation or the savings that could have been effected.
I think we have all been following some of the things that have been done. It will be recalled that the first Hoover commission was appointed in 1947. Perhaps it is also worth recalling that the first Hoover commission was given that name because its chairman was a former Republican president of the United States. He was appointed by a Democratic government in the United States. This indicates that there was certainly an impartial and objective inquiry.
That commission made its report and so well satisfied was the government with that experiment that President Eisenhower appointed the second Hoover commission in 1953. That commission has been reporting since then and already many reports have been received from the task forces that have been dealing with different subjects.
In regard to the report of the first Hoover commission, the New York Times, which I think most people will regard as one of the very responsible newspapers in the United States, said that 72 per cent of the proposals of the first commission appointed in 1947 had been either wholly or partially put into effect. Then also there was a very interesting organization set up in the United States, known as the citizens committee for the Hoover report. That voluntary committee sought to emphasize the need for efficiency and economy. That citizens' committee, made up of highly qualified people seeking efficiency in government, calculated that, of the 273 specific proposals put forward for more efficient and more economic administration of the government, 116 had been completely accomplished, 35 mostly accomplished, and 45 partly accomplished. The committee found also that, when the full effect of the proposals adopted had been felt, this would result in a monetary saving of at least $5 billion annually. I recall that figure because we have emphasized our belief that there can be large savings by an ordinary businesslike examination of the administrative figures of government and the general organization of government. Dealing with the organization of government, they found that $5 billion

Government Services
annually could be saved merely as a result of the carrying out of the recommendations of the reports of the first Hoover commission.
Then we come to the second commission, which was given very wide powers to examine various branches of government, and we find that the many reports which they have made suggest further substantial increases of a very striking nature. Again, to look at a very responsible newspaper in the United States, I find that the Wall Street Journal for May 20 of this year-and it is a very reputable financial publication-comments on the second Hoover commission under the heading "Hoover Says Commission to Make Suggestions for $13 Billion Saving". These are savings effected in a structure which expanded under forces and stresses very similar to those which caused the expansion here. The Wall Street Journal says that the taxpayers can be saved a total of $6 billion in regard to ordinary operating expenses and in addition that the treasury can gain a further $7 billion in moneys that are now being spent in connection with activities which could be better carried out, according to the Hoover report, by private enterprise in the United States.
Whether the figures are exactly comparable, at least let us remember that the first Hoover report resulted in proposals that actually called for savings and have resulted in large savings which, fully implemented, will reduce expenditures in this field by $5 billion a year, and that the second Hoover commission has made recommendations which would result in further annual savings of $6 billion a year. It is true that we cannot give the exact figures but, remembering that the United States is just a little over ten times as large as Canada, surely it is perfectly obvious that we could expect and would have reason to expect savings of the order of hundreds of millions of dollars if we carried out an appropriate examination of the general business of government in this country. That does not suggest for one moment that there is any dishonesty, that there is any misappropriation of funds or anything of that kind. When business experts go into any ordinary big private business and, as they often do, save hundreds of thousands or perhaps millions for the shareholders of those companies, they do that, not because there has been any misappropriation but because they have found that the business organization grew without effective integration of its activities and that, as a result of a more appropriate set-up, the avoidance of duplication and the better employment of the people actually engaged, they have obtained these results.

Now, let us remember that in this country, in addition to departments of government, we have many enterprises that will bear examination. Let us just look at the crown corporations which would bear examination. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation needs examination. I am talking about it from the business point of view on the basis of the reports of the Auditor General. The findings of the Auditor General make it perfectly clear that there should be an examination of the business structure, and its very unusual set-up would also suggest that. Then we have the Canadian farm loan board, the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National Railways Securities Trust, Canadian National Steamships Limited, Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Eldorado Aviation Limited, Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, Export Credits Insurance Corporation, Northern Transportation Company Limited, Northwest Territories Power Commission, Polymer Corporation Limited, Trans-Canada Air Lines. These are only some of the great corporations operated by the government, in regard to which every hon. member here is entitled to information. We know we are not able to get full information in regard to the Polymer Corporation. We know we are not able to get full information in regard to Canadian National Railways. We know we are not able to get full information in regard to Trans-Canada Air Lines. We know perfectly well we cannot get full information in regard to many of these because we are told that to disclose these facts would be placing those organizations in an unfair competitive position. If we accept that-and I certainly do not accept it-then the only hope we have is to have one of these objective examinations such as have been carried out in the United States.
I should also point out that another thing which the Hoover report dealt with in a very interesting way was the paper war that is carried on within their departments. It pointed out that there was an unbelievable waste of paper, to say nothing of the human effort involved. In the New York Times of February 21 of this year there was the following heading:	"Hoover Unit Bids U. S.
cut Red Tape to Save Millions". Of course, it is true we have had the statement, "What's a million?" But this is not a single million; this is millions. This is one of the things that are symptomatic of a general condition. The Hoover report already filed suggests better management of the paper work of government; and how forcefully it deals with some of these slick publications issued by government departments to extol the hidden

virtues of some of those associated with the various activities of those departments! Those reports make interesting reading, when we see the figures of transportation dealt with by the Hoover report. They indicate the wanderlust that gets into people once they find that there is nobody restraining their movements. There is nothing irregular, nothing unnatural, but if nobody is looking into the matter it is strange how distant fields not only look green but beckon so strongly that the farthest point to which a ticket can take one is the point that seems to be the most natural. Because of that the Hoover commission recommended that there be a director of transportation just to see if the trip really is necessary, and just to see also if there could not be certain savings. It also suggested certain directors to look into telephone calls, telegrams and communications of that kind. All of it has an astonishing similarity to what we see here in this country.
I do not propose to deal any longer with the Hoover reports because I know hon. members have read them, but there are so many things that suggest similarities. For instance, one of the task forces of the Hoover commission dealt with the fact there were so many architects in scattered offices here and there. Some of them did not know that other architects were doing exactly the same thing. It has already been commented on during the present session that there are 89 architects throughout the government services responsible to their respective departments but without any co-ordination of their activities under one central guiding body.
Then, what about the various activities of different departments which are precisely the same? What, for instance, about the national film board and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Let me refer to them as an example that could be extended over hundreds of examples, and I say hundreds, right across the board. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is now using a great many news films for its telecasts. We also have the national film board and private agencies taking news films. In many cases these people are taking the same news films on the same occasions. Surely if the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is going to be taking news and other films of that nature they could be the government agency to take that kind of film and supply them to the national film board or, if the national film board with its longer experience is the one to do it, then let them have the handling of them on the directive of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I cannot tell and no member of the government can tell at this time how much could be saved, but one thing is certain,
Government Services
that a great deal could be saved just by that one simple procedure. Other examples of that kind could be multiplied throughout the whole of the system.
There is another reason why I think there should be an examination. I think the time is overdue now for an examination of some of these agencies of government just to see where they fit into our private enterprise system. Let us really recognize that our economic system is a private enterprise system and that it is based upon the belief that the genius of individual effort and individual initiative provides the generative force which has given us the prosperity and growth that we have in this country. We should be very careful that, in a perfectly normal desire to meet emergencies, we do not create agencies which restrict that great human driving power which proved so successful during the last world war. If ever there was a real test of private enterprise it was the initiative of human beings brought up in a private enterprise economy who were able to adjust themselves suddenly to the dreadful demands of war and to improvise with all the initiative and ingenuity that arose under those conditions.
Then let us remember that these great public enterprises pay no taxes and little or no interest on their enterprises except for the special provisions which have recently been made. In the ordinary course of events they do not pay taxes such as are paid by private enterprises. I recognize there are exceptions, but the general principle is a limitation of taxes on publicly owned property.
Then there is very real evidence of a desire not to include depreciation in government accounting. That has been manifest in many of the accounts we have examined. However, without going into detail we do know that many of these organizations were built up under great pressure, and there should be an objective examination by an independent inquiry into the general set-up. We should be told whether these are in the best interests of Canada, and in the case of those that we know will and must continue to operate, like the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, both of which, I might say, were brought into existence by Conservative governments, we should have a re-examination and the whole system should be properly analysed to see where the impact on private enterprise is or is not appropriate, recognizing that we are a private enterprise country.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that just as in the case of private business we should examine them on a businesslike basis or we

Government Services
will encourage inflation. In fact, the government will get a vested interest in inflation unless it tackles this problem, because unless it does so the only way it will be able to meet some of the continuing obligations will be to encourage still further inflation by deliberately inflationary methods. Do not let anybody suggest that cannot be done because it has been done in country after country where they did not examine government business in the very manner that is being suggested here. Just think of all the countries of Europe which, a comparatively few years ago, thought their economies were as sound as a rock and whose currencies are debased today to a point where all the life savings of millions of people have been completely wiped out or, in the best of cases, substantially reduced in many of the countries.
We still have a chance but the time of grace is not too long. We still have a chance to examine our own affairs and to reverse the trend, to place the business of government on a sound basis. As I conclude these remarks I repeat my earlier suggestion which I placed before the government. If there should be a free vote, as we have had on different occasions, I would hope that hon. members, seeing what has been accomplished elsewhere to improve the general efficiency of government and the agencies of government, would support the motion I am going to place before the house. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question he deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that consideration should be given to the appointment of a commission of inquiry under part II of the Inquiries Act with powers to examine into and report upon the organization of the various departments of the Canadian government with a view to ascertaining and making recommendations respecting:
(a)	economies and improved services which could be effected by reorganization and elimination of duplication;
(b)	the status and function of crown corporations and other government agencies and their effect on our free enterprise economic system."
Six o'clock.
