speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I did not hear the hon. member because I was thinking of the amendment and some of the precedents that I was reading, while at the same time listening to the Leader of the Opposition. I may as well say now that it occurs to me this amendment deals with efficiency in government services. I should like hon. members to consider that during the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the acting leader of the opposition moved an amendment which appears on page 31 of Hansard for January 10, 1955. It reads in part as follows:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take or to recommend the necessary measures:
(d) to eliminate waste and extravagance in government and improve its efficiency.
Then on the budget the hon. member for Greenwood moved, at page 2954 of Hansard for April 19, 1955, the following amendment:
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that in its budget proposals the government has failed:
(c)	to curb its own extravagance and inefficiency.
The house will recall that, as recorded on page 3425 of Hansard for May 3, 1955, I issued a warning that questions that had already been decided by the house should not be offered for decision again in the same session. I referred hon. members to some rulings that had been given by my predecessors, namely Mr. Speaker Black and Mr. Speaker Macdonald, and also to two authorities on the point, Bourinot and Beauchesne. During the debate on the budget the mover of the amendment, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) did speak about the reduction of expenditures as recorded at page 2945. I see that in the same debate the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), who was the seconder of the amendment, spoke about what he called the fifth problem the budget ignored, the problem of waste and inefficiency. His words are to be found on pages 3396 and 3397 of Hansard for May 3, 1955. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) dealt with the point as well, and his words appear on page 3613 of Hansard for May 10, 1955.
I think I have said enough at the moment.

Since you have raised the matter now, and doubtless will be considering it, may I make a brief observation which I would not wish to suggest concluded my

remarks on the point. Each motion to which Your Honour has referred was a motion which expressed regret that certain things had not been done or sought a declaration that there was waste and inefficiency. Now, unless the defeat of those motions is to be taken as a declaration that this is the best of all governments and that they are flawless, I do not know how it would be possible to suggest to the house practical ways in which improvement in the business of this house should be carried out. We would be denied that opportunity.
After all, we are merely saying we want a committee set up to examine the business organization, to consider ways in which efficiency could be increased and savings effected, and the general aspects of our crown organizations in relation to private enterprise submitted to examination. I do submit that if resolutions suggesting waste and extravagance, and regretting that certain things have not been done, are voted down by a majority which finds it convenient to support the government, if that is going to wrap around the government such a veil of sanctity that we cannot even make practical suggestions for improvement, we really would have paralysed the business of this house.
Naturally, I leave that suggestion with you until this matter is under consideration again.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I point out to the Leader of the Opposition that when the acting leader of the opposition moved the amendment to the address in reply, I indicated to him at the time that each point mentioned in the amendment would be just that many blocking motions in the future. I felt the amendment was rather long. Now, later, when the amendment on the budget came along and we had another recital of various points which were a repetition of many of the points recited in the amendment on the address, I contented myself with issuing a caveat. In the first amendment on the address in reply we have words to the effect that the house regrets the government failed to eliminate extravagance and inefficiency. In the amendment on the budget the words were to the effect that the house regretted the government had failed to curb its own extravagance and inefficiency. Now, we have an amendment to the effect that consideration be given to the appointment of a commission to try to eliminate extravagance and inefficiency.
Now, the hon. the Leader of the Opposition has overlooked this point that the amendment to the address in reply, the amendment to the motion to go into committee of ways and means on the budget and this amendment on a motion to go into supply, are three want of
Government Services
confidence motions. When I issued the caveat a few days ago I was dealing with the amendment on the budget, and I referred hon. members to the Journals for Tuesday, November 22, 1932, page 113, a ruling by Mr. Speaker Black. It is not an isolated one but is one that fits the situation with which we are faced now perfectly.
Mr. Speaker Black had to give a decision on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means. To this an amendment was moved by Mr. Heaps as follows:
"In the opinion of this house it is desirable that a committee or commission be appointed to consider the economic situation in the dominion with special reference to unemployment and to report back during the present session of parliament."
A point of order has been raised that the amendment is out of order on the ground that it again introduces a matter that was debated and disposed of when the Right Honourable the Leader of the Opposition moved as part of an amendment to the address:
"The house regrets that, except the dole, the government has no policy with respect to the relief of unemployment."
Mr. Speaker Black continues:
I have carefully considered the arguments presented on the question of order, examined the authorities and precedents of both the British and Canadian houses of parliament. In the debate on the amendment of the Right Honourable the Leader of the Opposition to the address I find that he suggested that a committee or commission be appointed and given charge of the whole question of unemployment relief which shows that the subject matter of the proposed amendment was then open to discussion and actually debated. If this amendment is allowed it inevitably follows that there will be a repetition of the debate on unemployment.
The ordinary rules of debate are applicable on this occasion, for instance, a matter already decided by the house cannot be discussed. Bourinot 420
This amendment is offered on the motion to go into committee of ways and means and not being accepted by the government is a motion of want of confidence and the fact that it provides for the appointment of a commission or committee with special reference to unemployment is in effect a condemnation of the government's policy on that question.
The house has refused to condemn the government's policy on unemployment by rejecting the amendment moved to the address by the Leader of the Opposition.
In view of that decision by the house I cannot find that this amendment being a motion of want of confidence dealing also with unemployment is in order.
Now, the only flaw in this line of argument would be for the government to not consider this motion as one of want of confidence. Pending the time we hear from the government on that score, I shall reserve any further judgment. As it is six o'clock, I do now leave the chair.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the house a grievance having to do with agricultural matters.
I wish to continue the subject discussed this afternoon. I understand I may do so. Am I seen?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, Your Honour, I think I know the reasoning behind the desire of the hon. member for Greenwood to continue certain remarks. May I point out to you that there is a possibility that we-and when I say "we" perhaps I mean Your Honour-are confusing two things. On the motion to go into supply there are two kinds of speeches that may be made, namely, one, discussing public business and the other discussing grievances. We have followed the practice in this house, as I recall it, of Your Honour encouraging persons to continue the discussion of a grievance until it is exhausted, before proceeding to another.
As I apprehend the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon, the matter under discussion could not be described as a grievance; it could be described as a matter of general public business. That being so, it does not follow, I suggest, that we have to continue with the same subject. If it were a grievance, I suggest we should.

Mr. Speaker, on that point might I remind Your Honour that a ruling has been

made based upon the fact that it is related to what had been expressed in the form of a grievance or a complaint on an earlier occasion relating to a similar subject. To the extent that we have been able to establish that this was a form of public business unrelated to earlier complaints in regard to extravagance and waste, then, under the ruling that Your Honour made, and which it is not my intention to question at this point, we most certainly would have been in a different position from what we are now.
The rule, as I understand it, is that grievances may be raised. This was a grievance in the way in which the term is used to the extent that we placed before the house certain things that we thought should be done. It is quite proper to point out that we have placed the same thoughts before the house on other occasions in a different form, but, Mr. Speaker, I very strongly urge that the broad term of raising grievances covers the very point, and the only limitation is not that there be one class which is described as a grievance and another class which is described as a positive raising of public business, but rather that in raising grievances there may be only one motion. We have raised that motion. Your Honour has ruled it out of order. But I submit that it certainly comes within the broad term of grievance as used in relation to the rule that we are discussing, while we may ourselves have put it forward in a positive form.
Might I say, Your Honour, before you make a ruling, that of course there is also the fact that the leader of the house has divested himself of the opportunity to raise the argument that he now raises by saying that under no conceivable circumstances would he agree to a motion which was an amendment to the motion to go into supply. Consequently, he himself has established that this is a grievance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As I understand it, wide latitude is given to hon. members to air grievances on the motion to go into supply. The limitations are set out in citation 467 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, which says, in part:
. . . shall not relate to any decision of the house during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of ways and means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.
In connection with the first part of the citation that I read, which is to the effect that a grievance shall not relate to any decision of the house during the current session, hon. members know that sometimes grievances are put forward without any amendment being

submitted. That is citation 468. An amendment has been submitted which had the effect of directing the house to make a decision upon the amendment. I ruled the amendment out of order because in the main it dealt with a matter which had already been put in the form of an amendment on earlier occasions and decided upon by the house.
We are now in the same position, the amendment having been ruled out of order, as if no amendment had been moved at all. Until the Leader of the Opposition had moved his amendment, he had covered a wide field of government administration with respect to pointing out inquiries that should be made in order to strengthen the administration and also crown corporations that are agencies of the government. I am inclined to think that the discussion can go on on that particular subject matter, and any violations that I can foresee will probably have to be dealt with under standing order 40, subsection 2, which deals with repetition of arguments already used in previous debates which have been concluded, either by the hon. member who is about to speak or by other hon. members. But, as hon. members know, wide latitude is given with respect to grievances on the motion to go into supply, and I would hesitate very much at this moment to limit the discussion. I would rather see it go on, if that is the wish of hon. members, in the hope that there would be no repetition of the arguments that have already been used with respect to some of the points that may be brought forward at this time on the subject introduced by the Leader of the Opposition.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I hope that what I say will at least satisfy you that I am continuing on the line which you have approved.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, when I realize that what is happening is that we are suggesting to the government that they might improve their administration by getting the assistance of some experts to look at what they have been doing, I find it hard to believe that their answer is in the negative, or would have been in the negative, had it come to a vote. To me it seems so obvious that this would be a desirable course. Let us have a look at it. What is the situation of this nation's business? What kind of business is it that we are engaged in? After all, we are engaged in the biggest business that goes on in Canada by far. Well, of course, the first thing that strikes one about it is that it has grown enormously in the last 15 years. It has mounted by some 10 times or more. The second thing that strikes one about it-and this is a very unusual but a very important thing-is that it is a business where those 50433-271
Government Services
who are carrying it on can fix the income of the business. The income of the business is what they determine it is to be, and of course that in itself is a great hazard; that in itself is a great temptation to be easy-going with money, because, after all, if you do not have enough it does not mean you go broke; it just means that you get more money, as we are going to do this year because we are budgeting for a deficit.
I feel that when you consider the figures given this afternoon-I am not going to review them; I have heard them before; they were not new to me, and yet they struck me all over again-you have the feeling of what would happen if it was a private business. Well, of course, the answer is it could not happen; it would have been checked long ago. And so I repeat that all these things seem to me to indicate that an inquiry, assuming it is carried out by competent people, for people who are conscious of the need of help, who want help, could not be anything but a good thing. Of course, in private business it is the most natural thing in the world.
Let us have a look at these men in private business. Most of them have been in it all ttieir lives. They have been trained up to the job. It has been a matter of economic life or death to them. They naturally had to give everything they had in order to be a success; and yet they are only too ready to go outside and check up on what they have done. It does not mean that they abdicate their own judgment. I do not mean that they put themselves in the hands of some outside company because, as was pointed out to me by a shrewd observer this afternoon, sometimes the ideas of outside experts may be grandiose. Sometimes they may have extravagant ideas. Nevertheless, to have a check-up by an independent mind is good.
These heads of corporations are not weaklings; they are not men who have no selfconfidence; they are not men who are rushing off every day fearful of their own judgment and trying to substitute someone else's for it. They are men of self-confidence; but nevertheless they feel that from time to time it is wise to check themselves up from the outside, to get competent people to come in and look over what they are doing.
These efficiency companies do not just rise out of the air; they do not rise up without there being some field of want. People do not pay their high fees just for the fun of it, they pay their fees because they feel it is worth while to do so. They do so because they believe in having fresh and independent views. They want the truth, and there is nothing to prevent them getting the truth. Sometimes we in this house are a little

Government Services
handicapped by the fact that we know that we represent the views of other people, we know that we have to make our views palatable to other people and sometimes we may be a little handicapped in following an argument just where it leads. That makes it all the more important in my opinion that those who are engaged in the business of government should be ready and willing and anxious to get assistance from the outside.
What is the situation with regard to administration when we look at the cabinet?
I have proper respect for the cabinet and I think it worthy of some of the esteem in which its members hold themselves. Nothing that I say is intended to be derogatory. But I think it is also fair to say, and I think it is obvious to say that few ministers come into the departments with wide experience in administration. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was an exception.
What are the essentials of administration?
I suggest that a good administrator is a man who understands the advantages of delegation. That seems to be the key of the whole business. Delegation, I suggest further, means that he can pick good men, and that he will give them their heads, that he will give them plenty of responsibility and back them up. That is an awfully easy thing to say but it is extremely difficult to do.
I want to say another thing which most certainly can be said without any offence. We have a great many lawyers in the cabinet. I tried to be a lawyer once so that anything I say now cannot be regarded as derogatory to lawyers. But I say deliberately that it is only by an act of God that a lawyer is a good administrator, because after all-
You can say that again.

I believe that an act of God has been defined as an act that no reasonable man would take. As I said a moment ago, the essence of an administrator is that he knows how to delegate. But the essence of the whole life of a lawyer in practice is that of a man who does not delegate, it is that of a man whose personal services are wanted by his clients. I say with all respect and deference and regard for the profession that it is only an act of God if a lawyer is a good administrator.
I am not overlooking the civil servants who are there standing behind the ministers. There is no one that has more respect for them than I. They are trained men who have come up gradually, but on the other nand to some extent their life has been a secluded life. They have not had wide contacts with the world, they have not entered into tne rough
[Mr. Macdonnell.)
and tumble that people in business encounter. Furthermore I would be willing to hazard a small sum that if one could get a really freely expressed comment of the civil servant in the higher echelon as to whether he would like, however competent he may be in his own work, to have a check made by someone else looking at his work, he would get this reply, "Why wouldn't I?"
If he did not make such a reply then I would say that he is not as good a man as I thought he was. I would feel that he was conscious of some weakness, that he was not fully confident of his own work, that he was afraid or at any rate hesitant to allow an independent view to be brought in. Therefore I repeat that I think the highest type of civil servant would be all for an independent view. That adds strength to my feeling that it is desirable.
I come now to what I think is a most important point. I ask whether there have been any experiments, whether anything along this line has been done by the government. Of course the answer is that it has. I have here a report made several years ago in relation to the national film board, and hon. members will remember the reference that was made to the Woods-Gordon report in connection with the post office. In those two cases, for reasons which obviously I am not familiar with, there was a reference to an outside source. I want to refer to those because to me they offer the strongest possible argument in favour of what I am now arguing for.
If we had found in the case of these two reports that the investigators had no comment or criticism of any kind to make, then I think it might be said that that was prima facie evidence that my suggestion was unsound. It could then be said that when the government did do what I wanted them to do, when they did go outside to get allegedly expert people to make a report, they got a clean sheet. It is for that reason that I want to put on the record a brief reference to what was said about the national film board and also about the post office.
I suggest that if we find, as I shall suggest we do find, that these reports are critical, that they indicate all was not well; if we find, as I think we shall find, that these reports were the occasion of substantial and even drastic changes in the administration of these departments, then I shall feel that that is a strong argument for the argument I am making. I might just interject here, lest I forget, that it seems to me that what was said this afternoon by my leader about the Hoover report is in itself a very cogent argument.

We are extraordinarily like the Americans in many ways. When we find that they have spent the large sums of money which they did on those reports, when we realize the tremendous effort that has been put into the work implied by these reports, it seems to me that that is the strongest argument-putting it at the very lowest point-that we could find that that would be a useful course for us to follow.
I should like to refer briefly to some of the comments made with reference to the film board. The criticism was not strong, but nevertheless I think it warrants the time that anyone might spend in reflecting on it. This is a report by J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited, made by a man who I think has the respect of this house regardless of party. I submit that the suggestions made here are indications in connection with this small and rather tiny department which might be of tremendous importance in connection with the larger ones. Before I go on to the film board, I digress here to speak for a moment further about the huge department, the largest of all, the defence department. We have tried very hard here in this house to suggest to the predecessor of the present minister, who is a friend of us all, that he had a terrific job on his hands-he had over 30,000 civilian employees apart from the huge military staff-that it had grown like a mushroom and that it needed the most expert assistance that could be brought in. We did not get very far with the minister. The minister was capable of prodigies of individual work himself; he worked with almost feverish energy. I sometimes wondered if he did not think that if he worked as hard as he could, twice as hard as most of us, somehow or other that would do the job. At any rate when I pressed him and asked him how he was undertaking this huge addition to the work of the department, the answer I got was to the effect that there always has been a defence department, it has grown a bit certainly, but we are doing our job. I took that as said in good faith. If working, as I say, with feverish energy would have done the job, then I am sure it would have been done, but it left me with the feeling that there was no recognition of an obvious fact crying out for recognition, that here was a terrific job that needed special effort and special assistance.
Having said that about the Department of National Defence, I want to come back and read a short extract from this report on the film board because this is the kind
50433-271J
Government Services
of thing which if applied to the huge departments, should pay off with terrific results. This is the report made in 1950. I quote:
The administrative controls and procedures of the board have improved considerably in recent years but there is still room for substantial further improvement. Present shortcomings are mainly due to three causes: The business management section has lacked sufficient authority to control the expenditure of funds; the board has been obliged to work within the framework of government accounting practices which were not designed for a productive organization and are not suited to its needs.
I think that is a very important point. Here is a department of government which has gone into business and does not have the proper tools. I read further from page 24 of the report:
In the past, difficulties have arisen because commitments have been made without regard to the availability of funds; for example, in some cases: (a) Budgets have not been prepared until after the production of a film has commenced; budgets have been prepared to cover part of the work only;
I skip the rest and go down to (d):
Prints of films have been ordered by the distribution department without reference to the business management section as to the availability of funds.
I am not going to weary the house with further quotations. I submit that that proves exactly the point I am trying to make, that it could be of the greatest assistance to a department if some competent, reliable person of good sense were brought in and asked to give advice.
Now I wish to refer a little more at length to the Post Office Department, because, as we remember, a good deal more by way of criticism was said in regard to that. I am reading now from Hansard of January 15, 1954, page 1173:
With regard to the operations branch the report says-: "The work of the operations branch has over the years increased to the point where the staff at all levels are overloaded with a multitude of routine problems and correspondence. No one has had the time to develop policies which can be applied on an over-all basis."
Later on page 1173:
Here is one of the things the report has to say regarding controls:
"The branch is operating under a severe handicap as there are no standards established to measure the relative efficiency of a given method of operation. The lack of such standards is particularly felt when requests are received for additions to staff or accommodation."
One further quotation:
The cost information available to the department discloses that the special delivery service is operated at a considerable loss. In some centres the postal rate for a special delivery letter is less than the contractor is paid to deliver the letter. The user of the special delivery service is interested in a rapid and assured delivery. It is believed

Government Services that the majority of users would be prepared to pay considerably more for this service if their requirements were met.
Here is a statement of a condition which apparently was not known to the department.
I repeat it:
In some centres the postal rate for a special delivery letter is less than the contractor is paid to deliver the letter.
That is apart from all the work and overhead in the Post Office Department itself.
Now, I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that to me the arguments in favour of this seem convincing, and I have still to hear any argument against it. I cannot remember any real argument at all having been made against it. I would not undertake to say that no argument has been made, but certainly none that seems to me worthy of consideration. I would have thought that all the arguments were on the one side. The expense would be trivial and the possibilities of recovery enormous. As I say, it almost seems as if we on this side were not to be allowed to have any good ideas of any kind. The mere fact that we put something forward apparently is enough.

speechtext: My hon. friend knows we have often accepted good suggestions from the opposition.
I may have a poor memory, but I do not remember many.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Maybe there were not many.

It is open to the minister to say that they would have accepted them if they had been good; that is always open to him. But I will repeat that I hope very seriously that if this is going to be turned down we shall be given the reason. There may be good reasons, but I do not know them.
I remember a remark made in the New Statesman and Nation about Lord Beaver-brook. They did not think much of him, but they did say this, and I think it is applicable to the present situation. In the early days of the war they said that they would like to see Lord Beaverbrook put into every department of government for just two months. They meant that he would clear out all the cobwebs, that he would throw out all the preconceived ideas and make everyone re-think what they were doing.
It also reminds me of a story about Churchill when he became first lord of the admiralty as a young man-I think he was 37 at the time. He went all through the departments and asked all the people to tell him what they were doing. After they told him, he asked a question that they had never been asked before. He asked "Why?" That 

apparently was quite a shock to them. I suggest that something like that should happen here. I do not wish to derogate from the members of the cabinet, and I do not wish to derogate from the civil servants, for whom I have a great respect. I am talking about what I believe is an inescapable situation where things are allowed to run on from decade to decade. In some departments we would probably find that they were doing things because they did them in the time of Sir John Macdonald. I do not doubt that the things that were done in Sir John's time were wise, but that does not say that they are going to be wise 60 years later.
It seems manifest good sense to do this.
I should like to point out that this comes, not from a man without experience in administration. I should like to recall in passing that my leader was prime minister of Ontario for five years and, speaking for myself, I have never yet heard anyone of any party in Ontario say he was not a good prime minister. The suggestion comes from him and the rest of us support it and are enthusiastic about it. I hope it will not suffer the fate it had before, for I say, subject to being corrected, that I do not recall an argument being made against it. I say that to me this is manifest good sense. At the worst we will have spent a little money. Perhaps we will feel afterwards we did not get value received, but I do not fear that. There would be value received anyway because if no criticism were made the government could have the feeling that everything was all right and they could make use of it in the next election. I would take a chance on that myself. I would risk the government getting a clean sheet. Therefore I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that consideration should he given to the appointment of a commission of inquiry under part II of the Inquiries Act with powers to examine into and report upon the organization of the various departments of the Canadian government."

Mr. Speaker, I really had not anticipated entering this debate but since it has continued on the basis of the subject matter introduced in support of the amendment you declared out of order before the dinner recess, and since another amendment of a rather different kind has now been moved, I wish to say something about the subject matter surrounding the amendment. First of all I want to say that the members of the parliament of Canada are elected to do a certain job and when we are elected we assume

certain responsibilities. One of those responsibilities as far as the opposition is concerned and, indeed, private members on the government side too, is that we shall scrutinize very carefully expenditures of the government and proposals of the government for expenditures. It seems to me that is a fundamental duty of members of the House of Commons. I do not believe that at any time, unless the circumstances are very exceptional, we should abdicate those rights and powers that are properly the function of parliament.
It has been said of course that a somewhat similar commission was set up in the United States by congress under former President Hoover. But let me point out that the parliament of Canada and, indeed, the parliaments of the commonwealth of nations, are not comparable in many respects to the congress of the United States. In the House of Commons we have sitting before us every day of the week that we sit ministers of the crown who are responsible directly to the elected members who sit in this house. The advisers of the president of the United States, that is. the cabinet of the United States, are not members of congress. They are the personal choice of the president, are not responsible directly to the members of congress and do not occupy seats either in the Senate or in the House of Representatives.
Consequently the situation in the United States regarding the examination of accounts, the questioning of ministers and the inquiry into public matters of that description is essentially different in method from those that we adopt in the parliaments of the commonwealth, of which the parliament of Canada is one. One of the major responsibilities of the members of the House of Commons is that of inquiring into the expenditures of the government and satisfying themselves that those expenditures are being properly, efficiently and economically made. So I say that there is a fundamental difference in the approach to this problem between the United States and Canada.
Let it not be said that in saying this I am condoning in any way the extravagances which I believe can be found in government administration. This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) quite properly placed before the house a substantial list of very startling expenditures that, I suppose, had been prepared for him very carefully by persons in his office or elsewhere, and which indicated there were very large expenditures in certain fields that I do not think can be justified at any time.
For the last several years I have looked at the expenditures of the first department he mentioned today, the Department of
Government Services
National Defence. It is a very difficult thing for a member of the opposition or, indeed, any private member of the house, to rise and suggest that the estimates of the Department of National Defence should be cut by $100 million, $200 million, $300 million, $400 million or $500 million because, unfortunately, the Department of National Defence is surrounded by a veil of secrecy. If one endeavours to curtail the estimates of that department one is accused immediately of being opposed to adequate defence of our country. I think there is no individual, no person in this house, who would cripple our country in defending itself against the threat of aggression or actual aggressive action on the part of any country in the world.
Yet I say I am convinced in my own mind that the figures produced this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition confirm in part the opinion I have held for a long time that we could save $100 million, $200 million, $300 million or more if we could examine the expenditures of that department. Let us take travelling expenses. Personnel travel unnecessarily I think from one end of the country to the other by air or by train with all the facilities that the railways offer to travellers by train these days available to them. I am not complaining about that because when we send our young men across the country for training in the army, navy or air force I think they are entitled to as comfortable a trip as we ourselves like to have when we move from one end of the country to the other. But I am convinced that if the house could go into the expenditures of this and some other departments we could effect very considerable savings and economies.
Consequently let it not be said that in criticizing the proposal made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) or the proposal ruled out of order this afternoon I am in any way condoning any of the extravagances I am convinced could be discovered if this house constituted itself in a manner that would enable it to inquire into these expenditures very carefully indeed. We of the opposition, of course, have to take some blame ourselves. We have not endeavoured to have one of the standing committees of the house meet and function as it was intended to function. I refer to the public accounts committee. I do not think there has been a meeting of that committee this session. In my view that is rather scandalous, but I am not blaming the government alone for that. I think we of the opposition are equally to blame with the government if the public accounts committee does not sit and does not function properly. This afternoon and again

Government Services
this evening mention was made of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the necessity of inquiring into the expenditures of that organization. We get that opportunity almost every session. Almost every session a committee is set up. One was set up this session. What are the terms of reference? The terms of reference are that the report of the broadcasting corporation shall be referred to this committee for examination. The report of the broadcasting corporation, which includes a financial report, is sent to that committee.
What has that committee become? It has become an avenue of propaganda for the private broadcasting stations in this country. Almost the whole time of that committee is occupied in listening to criticism of the C.B.C. from the point of view of the private broadcasting companies or listening to propagandists for the Canadian association of broadcasters, the private organizations. That has been true over the years. If we on this side of the house are going to complain about alleged extravagances within the C.B.C., then let us indulge in a little self-examination to ascertain whether or not we have accepted the opportunities presented to us for an examination of the expenditures of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The same is true, of course, of many other organizations, organizations which, as the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon, were established by Conservatives. If there has been any lack of investigation into some of the financial operations of the government, then, as I said before, we of the opposition parties share a responsibility because we have not pressed adequately for the functioning of the public accounts committee. We share responsibility because, when the reports of the broadcasting corporation or some other corporation have been referred to a special committee, instead of going into the financial affairs of the organization most of the time has been spent in propaganda discussions as to whether or not the corporation should lose some of its powers and whether private interests should obtain greater privileges in that connection.
I am not going to criticize government expenditures except on the ground on which I have already criticized them, namely that I think there are extravagances and that sufficient economies are not effected by the government. I do not go along with the idea that government expenditures, because they are government expenditures, are inflationary. As a matter of fact, I would take the opposite position. I would say that if the government taxes the people of the country then they deny to the people of the country demands that might lead to scarcities and inflated
fMr. Coldwell.]
prices. We in this country are being very heavily taxed now. Secondly, if the government borrows from the savings of the people, and does not go to the Bank of Canada as in effect we did during wartime when such expenditures were inflationary, then that is actually deflationary because we are taking from the people by way of a loan the savings that they might otherwise spend in seeking consumable goods. If that money were spent in that form, it might conceivably lead to competition for commodities which would increase prices and bring about inflationary conditions. I am not, therefore, criticizing from that point of view. I take the opposite point of view in this respect.
I want to reiterate what I said at the beginning. I am convinced in my own mind that if this house functioned as it should, if the committees functioned as they should, and if we -were permitted to look into some of the departments of government where expenditures are mainly confidential and where many of the activities are classified or secret, we could effect considerable economies in those departments. As I said at the beginning, I have particularly in mind the one department which we cannot investigate fully, the Department of National Defence. I quite agree with the Leader of the Opposition when he says that accounts for telegrams and telephone calls and so forth are out of all proportion. As a matter of fact today I can mail a letter from this House of Commons at noon, and it will reach my own constituency nearly 2,000 miles away the next day.
That is the post office.

The Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Pickersgill) takes a bow. I do not believe he has anything to bow about. If he were on his job he would canvass the government departments to see that they spent more money on air mail and less on telephones and telegrams. I do not believe my hon. friend has anything to bow about in that regard. It always amazes me that something this parliament does-and it was this parliament which authorized the all-up carriage of first class mail, this parliament did it and not the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) or the Acting Postmaster General or the government-
On the recommendation of the government.
It was this parliament that authorized the doing of this particular thing. The government recommended it but that does not say-
And the hon. gentleman opposed it.
The Liberal majority put it through.
I did not oppose it. I am one of the "hon. gentlemen opposite", and I did not oppose it.
Did you not oppose the Postmaster General's bill last year?

That was concerned with something else, and not the carriage of air mail. Sometimes it seems that hon. members will take a vote or a speech by a member on this side of the house and twist it around to suit their own convenience. I think that is what the Acting Postmaster General is trying to do now.
Let us get our history straight.

I am not going into the history of anything of that nature because I might make a mistake in the date. I do not want to have to rise tomorrow afternoon and correct an error of that description in Hansard, because I, too, taught history for quite a long time.
I do not agree with the idea of setting up a commission which in effect would be an abdication by this parliament of its responsibilities and rights. I cannot support that point of view. The time may come when this parliament may become so ineffective that we may have to do something of that sort. But in spite of the fact that, as I fear, and have felt for some time, this parliament has not been functioning as it should function, and moreover that it does not command the respect of the people of Canada that it should command, I do not agree with the idea of setting up a commission. I feel the fact that parliament does not command the respect of the people is not the fault of parliament itself. I feel it is the fault of the electors. If, over the last few years, the electors had sent here a house which was more evenly divided-no matter how divided-
Had sent a Conservative government.

As a matter of fact, the best parliament for dealing with problems of this description and other problems in which I ever sat was the parliament from 1945 to 1949, when the government had a relatively small majority. Both the opposition and the government kept on their toes during those four years. That was the best parliament in which I had sat; and this is my fifth parliament. And I say it is not altogether the fault of members of the house, but rather the fault of the people who have made it impossible,
Government Services
because of the smallness of the opposition, for the opposition to function perhaps as it should function.
I think of the manner in which committees are set up. Just look at this house tonight, and it becomes clear that several members are not here. And that is because committees are sitting tonight. One of those committees has been sitting all day-morning, afternoon and evening. Sometimes as many as three or four committees are sitting at the one time.
I would like to see more committees of the house; but that would necessitate a larger representation on the opposition side of the house. Because, while the government has plenty of supporters to fill those committees- and they make sure that they do fill them, in the literal sense-the opposition is in a very different position.
So I say, then, that I am not in favour of abdicating the functions of parliament by setting up a commission. I think what the opposition should be doing-and I am talking about all members in the opposition, not just the official opposition-is to demand that the public accounts committee should sit and that it should sit early in the session. I say that there should be sittings of the committees examining reports involving large expenditures, reports like that of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and that such committees should devote more attention to the balance sheets and less to the propaganda involved. And may I say I am very glad to hear someone sitting near me say that they spent more time on the balance sheets this year. I am glad to hear that.
But there are other committees that could be doing the same sort of thing. Let me say in conclusion that I wish to see every extravagance ended. As a matter of fact, if I may pay a compliment, I am thinking of one of the facilities that comes under the direction of Mr. Speaker himself. I have in mind the reading rooms of the Senate and the House of Commons and the great quantities of journals that come to those libraries and to the various departments of government. After careful study these have been cut down, more or less on the recommendation of Mr. Speaker himself, although I know that our committee did approve the recommendation.
True, that is a small saving; but there are major savings many times as great that could be undertaken if a thorough review were made by the house of the expenditures of the various departments. I would like to see this parliament function as a parliament should function, and one of the first duties of parliament is to examine carefully expenditures of government.

Government Services
Up to the present time how many estimates have we had before the House of Commons? There have been very few indeed. We have not had, for example, the estimates of the Department of National Revenue, nor have we had the estimates of the Department of National Defence. We are at the present time considering in the standing committee the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, but we have not begun to examine defence expenditures.
Beginning next Monday we are to have morning sittings, which means that the government hopes that within four or five weeks we may prorogue. Yet up to this time we have only begun one of the major functions of parliament, namely the careful examination of past expenditures and those for the current fiscal year.
And so, while I am not in favour of adopting the American plan, because American plans do not suit parliamentary institutions of the commonwealth, I am very much in favour of doing everything the house can do to curtail expenditures when they are extravagant. Because an expenditure which is not extravagant, an expenditure efficiently made, is often worth while.
How do you know?
I said that an expenditure that is not extravagant is worth while.
How do you know?

Well, I would want to examine it. I am not even saying that I would know it was worth while. I have simply stated the fact that a worth-while expenditure is not an extravagance. In making that statement I am not judging as to what is or is not worth while. I am stating what, in Euclid, we called a self-evident truth.
Res ipsa loquitur.

And so, Mr. Speaker, I leave the matter with the house. I, personally, shall not support the amendment because I believe we cannot abdicate the responsibility the people of Canada have imposed upon us as members of parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only a moment or two in this debate. There are one or two things I would like to say in support of the amendment, because I feel it is both sensible and sound. I do not think the proposal is suitable only to Americans just because the government of the United States has adopted it. Certainly there are many large businesses in Canada, which have, at

one stage or another, called in efficiency experts to see whether a job is being done well.
The Hoover commission in the United States did an exceptionally good job for the Eisenhower government. They showed where literally millions of dollars could be saved. I see no reason whatever why, if a similar commission were set up in Canada, it also could not recommend many savings the government could make.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has suggested that the scrutinizing of expenditures is a duty of members of parliament, and particularly of opposition members. Of course it is; but government has grown so tremendously in recent years that it is physically impossible for opposition members to scrutinize these expenditures with the necessary care.
This year we have been sitting since early in January. I wish to point out that the estimates of only three departments, totalling $189 million, have been passed. This means that we still have $4-3 billion to pass within the next three or four weeks. I say that rushing through the estimates at the last moment is not good enough. But I do not think it is necessarily the fault of opposition members. I give the government credit this year for having set up the estimates committee, to which three departments were referred. I think that committee did excellent work, but I believe it is only a beginning. The government should go much farther. Perhaps it would not be presumptuous on my part to suggest that next year every department of government should be referred to one standing committee or another.
For instance, finance, national revenue and trade and commerce could go to the standing committee on banking and commerce. Perhaps agriculture and immigration could go to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. Perhaps defence, defence production and veterans affairs could go to a special defence committee. Then, labour estimates could go to the committee on industrial relations, those of the Department of Transport to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. The estimates of the Department of Fisheries could go to the standing committee on marine and fisheries, and so on.
In other words, in my opinion, the estimates for every department of government should go to one standing committee or another for scrutiny before they are brought to the house. Moreover, I believe that every crown corporation owned by the government of Canada, should come before one standing

committee or another. At the moment I am thinking of organizations such as the Bank of Canada, the Polymer Corporation, Crown Assets Disposal Corporation; Canadian Arsenals, the Canadian farm loan board, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the printing bureau, Canadian government elevators, and so on.
Most of those organizations have not been before any parliamentary committee in the ten years I have been here. I do not think that is an efficient way for the government to run the people's business. If the estimates were referred early next session, as soon as the debate in reply is concluded, they could be given a much more thorough scrutiny.
Another point which I desire to make is that the opposition, which is so divided and weak at the moment, should be given experts to help them look over these various accounts. I do not think it would cost the taxpayers of Canada very much money to hire eight or ten economic experts to help us on the various committees to expertly scrutinize the estimates. I am sure such an expenditure would be returned many times over.
But even if the government adopted these proposals, I imagine there is still room for a commission such as the Hoover commission. Members simply have not the time, they have not the facilities, they have not the technical experience required to go over estimates thoroughly. I say that they would be helped in their duty by the kind of commission which is suggested in this particular amendment.
I wonder if there is an hon. member who thinks that in the expenditure of $4,500,000,000 there are not places where there is waste and extravagance. I know that there are some members of the government who have done their bit in the last year to cut extravagance. I would give the first credit to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). There are 22 vacancies in the Senate. He has not filled them. It is a good saving. I suppose it amounts to about $220,000 a year. Including office help, it may amount to $300,000. If further vacancies occur and are not filled, perhaps we can save additional money. I give the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) credit for saving fairly substantial sums. He cut down on the C.B.C. foreign service by about $500,000; he reduced the grain subsidy $1,500,000; the gold subsidy, $4,800,000. He cut down on the maple sugar subsidy, $400,000. He is taking steps in the right direction though I still do not think he has gone far enough. There are a good many other places where we can save money.
Mr. Speaker has done much in effecting savings in these parliament buildings. I have always maintained that here in the nerve 50433-272
Government Services
centre of government, in these buildings, the taxpayers should be able to expect reasonable economies. Unfortunately there are still a good many departments which are duplicated. I give the Speaker great credit for having amalgamated the post offices of the Senate and the House of Commons. I hope he is going to continue along the same lines with other duplications. There are still about 25 other departments in these very buildings which are duplicates, such as the police forces, the reading rooms, the barber shops, the stenographic pools, the journals offices, the debates offices, and so on. I hope, sir, that you will keep on with the good work you have done, and carry out your job to its logical conclusion. Let me express the hope that the members of the other place will give you every co-operation.
There is one place in particular where I think a committee of the nature suggested by the hon. member who moved this amendment could do very useful work. Over the years our estimate books have contained a great many subsidies. I am quite prepared to admit that once a subsidy is commenced, usually because of an emergency, it is very hard to get rid of it, even if the emergency has ended. There are literally dozens of subsidies in the estimates book. During the supper hour I looked through the various departments, and would like to mention a few. For cold storage warehouses there is a subsidy of $500,000; there is a grain subsidy of $15,500,000; there is a maple sugar subsidy for pails to the amount of $100,000; there is a C.B.C. subsidy to the amount of $18,000,000; there is a coal subsidy of $10,000,00; there is a gold subsidy of $11,000,000; there is a subsidy on government annuities of $1,300,000; there is a butter subsidy of about $1,225,000; there is a subsidy to McGill University for a coal gas turbine of $100,000. Many of these may be useful; many of them are probably desirable.
Hear, hear.

But I do think that once these subsidies have been put on the books, from time to time somebody should review them, and make certain that the original need continues. An outside body, not having to worry about the political results, could go over these subsidies and make recommendations to parliament as to whether or not any could be discontinued, or whether there was room for reduction in some particular item.
Of course, it is too late this session for such a committee to be set up, but I for one wish to join with the mover of this amendment, in hoping that the government will take such action at the next session. It would be sound business practice.

Government Services
Mr. Speaker, one cannot help but recognize the continuation of that good sense which the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre has been showing recently-
In getting fluorescent lighting in his office.

-in the remarks which he has just finished, and what I have to say to some extent will parallel what he has already said. The problem before the house is the essential problem of the house in committee of supply, namely, that of seeing that value is received for the dollars that are spent. It has been said that everybody's property is nobody's property. No doubt public property, which is everybody's property, is the responsibility of this House of Commons, and no one wishes to detract from that responsibility. It is clearly recognized. The control of parliament with respect to the purse is clear under our constitutional history, and the control of the purse has been the control of the executive. There is no question of abdication; there is no question of parliament shirking its responsibilities. The question before the house is how that responsibility can best be exercised.
It is true that the ultimate decision and choice rests with parliament; but there are many ways that it performs this function with respect to the purse. What we are considering tonight is an aid to parliament. Parliament has aids which we all know of and use. The Auditor General makes a constant scrutiny of the expenditures of the departments to make sure that they comply with the authority given by parliament for those expenditures in the various votes, and his report is a report to parliament on what he finds.
Then, of course, the house attempts to discharge that responsibility of seeing what value it is getting for the expenditure of the money. As has been pointed out, it is a task that is somewhat beyond the time and capacity of the house as a committee of the whole. Perhaps we have four weeks to go, and the amount that is still to be voted is a large proportion of a very large budget of between $4 billion and $5 billion.
I should like to refer to the assistance that was given to parliament by means of the special estimates committee this year. As I sat on that committee, I think I can properly say that to my mind at least it had the opportunity to inquire in greater detail about the work of the departments which came before the committee, the expenditure of the money which had been voted for those
[Mr. Thatcher I
departments, and of the activities and results which arose out of that expenditure. But, as has been said here, the possibilities of that kind of inquiry are limited. One of the greatest limitations is that of party solidarity. In that special estimates committee the opposition are naturally the most critical of the government's expenditures of money, and why should they not be? The government itself is not anxious to bring out of the closet those skeletons that may be there, and therefore they are very careful to keep the door as tightly closed as possible, both in the House of Commons and in these committees.
As I said, the solidarity of the support which the government gets from its own followers is such that the opposition minority in the house or on a committee, while it is ready to work and seek information, is not always successful in getting it. As a matter of fact it is quite the contrary. While the special committee on estimates was a useful inquiry into routine departmental administration, I suggest that it did not fulfil the purpose which is envisaged by this motion.
That purpose is to have an objective inquiry by a non-partisan commission outside of the house, not composed of members of either the government or the opposition but of disinterested experts who would have the right to inquire and to receive information of all kinds which is necessary to come to conclusions and make the recommendations which should be made.
It has been suggested that this is in fact a proposal that parliament abdicate its responsibility. I think what I have said so far indicates my viewpoint on that, that parliament is in no sense abdicating. It retains its ultimate control, but it has need of the various aids and assistance which have been suggested. More particularly it needs the aid of the objective outside inquiry which has been proposed in this motion.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) says that we are copying United States precedents which have no application here, which are not needed and which in fact would indicate an abdication by parliament even if in the United States the Hoover commission has been able to perform a useful function. As everyone knows, congress is a good deal more independent of the executive than is parliament. Everyone knows that committees, both of the House of Representatives and of the Senate, exercise very wide powers. Those committees can seek and obtain information. In spite of that framework for inquiry we find that the Hoover commission was able to recommend substantial economies which none of these committees had discovered.

I suggest that the government itself has recognized the virtue of this proposal. It has proposed an inquiry by a commission outside of parliament into the economy of the country. That is no different in kind from what is suggested with respect to the administrative machinery of the government. Further, the government has recognized the virtue of this proposal in part by the inquiries which it has commissioned by private investigators into various departments of government.
Hon. members will recall some of those inquiries. There was the inquiry which was discussed last year into the Post Office Department by a firm of business experts or engineers. There have been a good many inquiries commissioned by the government to assist those public servants who are charged with the administration of departments. Those inquiries have been able to make suggestions for improvement in the methods of administration and for economy.
This is what one would expect would come out of a private inquiry reaching into all departments of government and having a view of the administration of the federal government as a whole. I said that there were some very good reasons why a private view is necessary. In the course of the examination of certain departments this year there were some very notable instances of the overlapping of the functions of civil servants in one department with those of civil servants in another. There is ample scope for the co-ordination of the activities of many departments which cross each other's paths. Therefore it seems to me that an over-all view, which would be an extension to some extent of what the government has been doing already in connection with individual branches or offices or departments, would pay large dividends to the people of Canada in economies and in efficient administration.
Another reason why the suggestion is timely is to be found in the course taken by public finance in this country in the last five years. The predecessor of the present Minister of Finance followed a policy which produced undeclared or unpredicted surpluses, or at least surpluses of undeclared proportions and unpredicted size in each of several years. That method of budgeting was not a deliberate production of surpluses for the purpose of reducing the public debt; at least it was not the avowed production of surpluses to reduce the public debt. If it had been, one could have understood and approved of it as an example of cyclical budgeting on the theory of surpluses in good times with the possibility of deficits in less good times. But that was not the declaration or the admission of the Department of Finance.

So we had in effect large surpluses produced which were not expected and which I think were to some extent embarrassing because they had not been predicted. Of course in circumstances where there is money lying around there is always someone ready to devise a method of spending it or to make use of it for one scheme or another which may be his particular hobby. Civil servants are no different from other people in that respect.
I suggest that the fiscal policy of this country during the last five years, producing as it did unexpectedly large surpluses which were not appropriated for the purpose of debt reduction but which just had to be expended as an unexpected surplus, which had to be spent, meant a debauching of the public service of the country by leaving around too much money for them to expend.
Every man in a job likes to do as well as he can. That often involves the expansion of staff and the increase of functions. The thing snowballs until we have departments which today are spending twenty times what they were spending ten years ago. Many departments have been through an experience of that kind. Many of them not only have had an experience of that kind but they have had the experience of the opportunities that came with war. In the case of those who administered the Department of National Defence, all one had to do was to ask and he would receive. No one questioned expenditures directed to the winning of the war. But that kind of attitude toward public funds which can develop in wartime must be checked eventually. I suggest that the government has never faced that issue and we still have a Department of National Defence which feels that all it has to do is to ask and it will receive.
With that immediate background to public administration in this country, it seems to me that this is a most opportune time to ask for the sort of inquiry which has been suggested. Ordinary expenditures of government have risen from $500 million in 1939 to $2,500 million today, five times what they were a bare sixteen years ago. Taking into account the expansion of the country, the inflation of the dollar and a number of other things, there is still a great deal of inflation in the expenditures of the departments themselves, which deserves inquiry to satisfy the house that it is getting value for its dollar. It is the responsibility of the house to be satisfied. This is a method by which it can be satisfied. It is a means by which the house can more effectively discharge its responsibilities.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house calls for the appointment of a commission-I quote from the motion itself-"with powers to examine into and report upon the organization of the various departments of the Canadian government". If that is all that the motion seeks to accomplish, it certainly does not bear out the intention of those who have spoken so far in respect to government expenditures or extravagances, because it does not refer to extravagance and it does not even refer to expenditures. It has to do with the organization of the various departments of the Canadian government. All that that commission would be in effect is an advisory committee to the Prime Minister, because the Prime Minister is the one who is responsible for the organization of the various departments. He is responsible for the appointment of the various ministers who head those departments, and of course the ministers in turn take the responsibility for the internal organization of the departments over which they are head. So all this motion would accomplish if it passed would be to set up an advisory committee to the Prime Minister giving him advice as to how the various departments should be set up. On that basis, of course, it falls far short of any inquiry in the real sense of the word into extravagance or expenditure and for that reason, I believe, is quite inadequate to the situation which is being discussed.
However, I realize that behind the motion is the intention, as expressed by various members so far, of trying to find out and correct any extravagances which may be found in government. But it should be clearly understood that there is a differentiation between extravagance or waste or inefficiency on the one hand and expenditures as such on the other. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher), who spoke a few moments ago, did not seem to understand the distinction or did not see fit to state so, because in trying to justify his criticism of inefficiency and extravagance he used examples which had nothing to do with inefficiency and extravagance at all. They had to do with government policy, or rather with policy passed by this parliament. He referred to subsidies, for example, the feed grain subsidy and that on butter. That has nothing whatsoever to do with inefficiency and extravagance; it is the carrying out of a policy laid down by this parliament. The government is doing something which parliament has authorized it to do. It is doing that efficiently. If it is paying out these subsidies in an efficient manner, then there is no extravagance or inefficiency involved
[Mr. Michener I
at all in the matter. If there is inefficiency in the administration of those subsidies, then to the extent that there is inefficiency there is waste.
But the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre was not complaining about any inefficiency; as a matter of fact he was complaining about too much efficiency in the paying out of subsidies, because he wanted the subsidies cut down and he wanted less subsidies paid out. This is rather a strange position to take, because he could have gone on to cite the greatest example of a subsidy in this country, which would eclipse altogether all the little ones he has mentioned. He could have mentioned the Canadian tariff structure, the biggest subsidy in the history of Canada, a subsidy which makes all the other subsidies look like peanuts. It is a subsidy which is the umbrella under which manufacturers have been operating, the chief among the beneficiaries, of course, being the hardware business. If we are going to talk about subsidies as such, we would have to begin with the tariff structure and work our way down to these other things, rather than begin with the little things.
I would like to see that tariff abolished too.
I may have a convert.
He will be back with you, the first thing you know.

Seriously, to come back to the motion itself, it is necessary to differentiate clearly in our minds and in our presentation here between the expenditure as such authorized by parliament on the one hand and waste and extravagance on the other. If we do not do that, we shall leave a false impression in the minds of the public. Statements have been made that parliament is not always looked upon very kindly by the public. Quite often it is parliament that is to blame, not because of the way it carries out its duties but because of what members say about themselves. If we leave the impression that every time we pay a subsidy or make an authorization of exoenditure which runs into hundreds of millions, for example, national defence, which runs into billions, we are wasting money and being extravagant, we deserve to be criticized, but we are leaving a false impression. Every expenditure is passed by parliament, and if that expenditure is made efficiently then there is no extravagance involved; it is a simple business operation. But there are legitimate cases of extravagance and waste, and that is what we have to go after.
I can give one example of extravagance of which I would like to hear an explanation

by the Minister of Finance or some other person authorized to give it. For example, recently I received a return in which it is shown that three cabinet ministers have permanent passes on the T.C.A. which permit them to use the facilities of the T.C.A. at any time anywhere. To my way of thinking, in the first place that is quite unnecessary, and in the second place quite unfair. There is no justification for it. If the government can justify that kind of thing, then I should like to hear the explanation. Some may say that after all we are not throwing money away but we are just giving free rides to these ministers, but at the same time it costs money to transport people. There are three cabinet ministers, all of whom, I assume, have expense accounts, and on every legitimate trip they make on government business they are legally permitted to put that down on the expense account and that is paid for. What purpose can be served by giving those three ministers permanent passes which permit them to fly to any part of the world where T.C.A. flies, whether it is on government business or for a fishing trip or any other purpose? It might even be for the purpose of speaking at an election campaign somewhere.
They would not do anything like that.

No, they would not. To my mind that is one type of expenditure which is an extravagance and a waste, for which the taxpayer is paying, and which is absolutely unnecessary and unjustified. There should be an explanation for it. I could give other examples, but our greatest disability lies in what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), my leader, expressed as the veil of secrecy. It is a serious matter. It is a matter about which a great many taxpayers today are beginning to ask questions, and they are quite justified in asking those questions. For example, when we say we are spending approximately $2 billion a year for national defence they want to know just what we are getting for the $2 billion. They are not saying it is too much or too little. They are in no position to say that any more, if I may be permitted to say so, than we are because we are not able to get the information they want. They want to know, when we authorize an expenditure of $2 billion, how many planes, how many tanks and other types of equipment we are getting for the money, the cost of each unit, where the money is being spent, how it is being spent, and to what extent it is necessary for the defence of Canada.

When we try to get that information we are told that a great deal of it is not available because it is of a secret nature and to reveal it might result in giving information to the enemy. I for one certainly would not advocate anything which would result in any potential enemy of Canada obtaining information it could not get otherwise. But I am afraid that at times we "kid" ourselves if we think that the kind of information we need in order to justify that kind of expenditure is the kind of information that the potential enemy either does not have or cannot get.
When it is a question of the cost of the equipment, the way in which government contracts are granted, the margin of profit on such contracts and so on, these are not matters of a military nature. However, if the government feels some danger is involved in informing members of the House of Commons of the details of national defence I suggest

I for one would be prepared to do this although others may not-the setting up of a committee of the house whose meetings would be held in camera. It could be made perfectly clear that the information would only be revealed in confidence and if the government insisted I would be prepared to take an oath of secrecy with respect to such information as, in the opinion of the government or in my opinion, would be of value to the enemy.
But I am quite satisfied in my own mind that the things we would like to know about expenditures on national defence are not the kind of things that would be of any value to anyone except as information to the Canadian taxpayers. That is one way in which a great deal more of detailed information could be given. Then we as members of the house would be in a position to judge and would be able to inform the taxpayers of Canada whether their money was being efficiently handled.
Another department with respect to which we are under the same disability, and this matter has been mentioned recently on a number of occasions, is the Department of National Revenue. Under the terms of the Financial Administration Act that department is authorized to make refunds or remissions of taxes. I was going to say "kickbacks" but that might be the wrong word. Only recently certain remissions were made to private corporations amounting to approximately $2 million, a considerable amount of money at any time. We have sought to obtain an explanation of the reasoning leading to the making of these remissions which, after all, involved the giving back to private
