The information already
asked for has been refused by virtue of the secrecy provisions of the Income Tax Act. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is partly right when he states that the Minister of National Revenue promised to give an explanation of the particular case to which I referred during the discussion of his estimates, but the minister will recall that previously I asked by way of a return for the correspondence dealing with the dispute between the department and the companies concerned in that case, which is actually the information needed to enable us to pass upon the case and decide whether the money was remitted to these companies in a proper manner. That information was refused by the Minister of National Revenue on the basis of the secrecy provisions of the Income Tax Act-again the veil of secrecy.
These are the kind of things that make it difficult for us to obtain the necessary information in order for us to be able to judge these matters. May I say here that I am not criticizing anyone in particular because I am sure all members of the house, whether on the opposition benches or sitting behind the government, want to have factual information about every dollar that is spent because, after all, it is the taxpayers' money that is being spent. We represent the taxpayers so that we have an inherent right to that information, but we cannot obtain it.
Before leaving this matter there is one thing more I should like to point out. Quite often we talk about inefficiency and extravagance when we speak of government expenditures, and it is quite legitimate to do so. After all, this is the forum of the country. But

I would not want to leave the impression that the only place where there is inefficiency or extravagance in the handling of money is in connection with government expenditures because to do so would be to leave a wrong impression in the public mind. I am quite convinced, and I am sure those who are familiar with private business will agree with me, that in the huge privately owned financial and industrial corporations of this country there is a great deal of extravagance and inefficiency, but because it is not something in which the public are directly interested it is never brought to light. It is also said it is no concern of ours.
For example, if the Ford Motor Company or General Motors wasted $500 million we would say they were wasting their own money so why should we care, but if the government wastes $100 we want to know why. That is perfectly true so far as our direct responsibilities are concerned, but let us not forget we have an indirect responsibility so far as private business is concerned. If a huge corporation, through inefficiency, extravagance or for some other reason, wastes a few million dollars that amount of money must be charged to the consumer who buys their product. This is an indirect form of taxation which every consumer must pay, and therefore I should like to see an inquiry into price spreads which would help to bring to light waste, extravagance and inefficiency in private administration as well as in public administration.
I say that in passing-of course it cannot be done under the terms of this motion-in order to make it clear that when we speak of waste, extravagance and inefficiency in the administration of government we should be careful not to leave the impression that all government administration is wasteful, extravagant or inefficient, because that is not the case. Any government, particularly a government that has been in power too long and has perhaps become a little bit slow at the switch, is in danger of allowing inefficiency and extravagance to creep into its administration.
If members of the house had the opportunity to obtain the kind of information which they want, I think they could pass judgment on government expenditures without the necessity of having any kind of commission. As I said at the beginning, I am not particularly opposed to a commission if it can perform a useful function. But the motion calls for an examination and report upon the organization of the various departments of the Canadian government. In my opinion, that does not begin to touch the question of waste or extravagance. It could,

as is suggested here, add a little to the cost of government because after all the government would have to pay for the commission. In my opinion, that does not fill the bill.

should like to approach this problem in a more practical way from the standpoint of the government expenditures that have been referred to in the course of this debate. This afternoon my leader referred at considerable length to the amount of money that has been spent by various departments. Tonight we have had a differentiation made between those types of expenditures which take the form of subsidies and those which might be involved in connection with direct payments to maintain government departments.
I think the last speaker, to a great extent, used the same terms as were used by the Financial Times in its issue of about a week ago in discussing an address by Mr. Harvey Perry of the Canadian Tax Foundation. The article reads:
The conclusion to be drawn from Mr. Perry's review of the tax situation is that we are today merely paying the piper. The people wanted family allowances; and they got them. They wanted old age pensions; and they got them. They may not particularly want defence expenditures; but it is incumbent upon the government to undertake them in the interests of the people.
Now, this type of expenditure is the type that ordinarily we can expect will continue. When we talk about a commission to inquire into the expenditure of government funds, then I think the last speaker made no differentiation between those items in which we may expect economy and those in which we may expect continuing payments, perhaps even on a larger scale. As a matter of fact, it seems that there should be no reason why we cannot approach the business of government in the same manner as any businessman approaches the problems in his own business. I believe that if we referred to the problems which arise in connection with production methods and controls, we could find a very good example to follow in connection with expenditures by government departments.
The practical situation is this. When someone is setting up a production line for a particular product he expects that, with continuing production, he may cut down his over-all cost of production. The larger his production runs the more economies he may expect. Apparently this is not true in connection with government departments because we have seen increasing expenditures far out of proportion to the increase in our population or even in proportion to the decrease, if I might use that term, in the value

of our dollar. In looking at some of the figures I might refer to a publication entitled "The National Finances" published by the Canadian Tax Foundation for the year 1954-55. We might take a good look at this to see what is happening in connection with government administration. I shall probably follow the figures through a little more closely than my leader did this afternoon.
In 1939, professional and special services cost this country $4 [DOT] 1 million. Now, I think we could say that since that time our population has increased approximately one-third or even 50 per cent. We might say that professional and special services should now amount to $8-2 million. Then, economists will tell you that your dollar is only worth 50 cents today, so that $16 million might be a reasonable figure to spend on professional and special services under today's conditions in relation to the amount that was spent in 1939. However, we find that this government estimates it will spend $31 million in that category in 1955.
Travelling and removal expenses, if we applied the same principle of allowing for the additional people who must be looked after and doubling the amount to cover the decrease in the value of our dollar, would probably result in an expenditure of approximately $8 million on the basis of the 1939 figure. However, we find that the estimate for 1955 is $15 million. This trend continues right through the list. Telephones, telegrams and other communication services amounted to $700,000 in 1939. It might rise to $2 million under the formula which would relate it to the 1939 figure. Instead, we find it rises to $6-7 million for 1955. Advertising amounted to $1-8 million in 1939. Using the same formula we probably should arrive at a figure of perhaps $3 million. We find that the estimate for 1955 is $8-1 million.
This is a fairly large sum to spend on advertising. As a matter of fact, we have set ourselves up in government at a pretty high price. I have here a list of the amounts spent on advertising by the leading firms in this country. The authority is the Toronto Star records department. I find the largest amount spent by any corporation in Canada last year was $688,031. However, we apparently use advertising services in this government to the tune of approximately $8-1 million, perhaps 10 to 12 times as much as the largest corporation in Canada spends on advertising today.
If we apply the production type technique and if we, as an illustration, look at such items as the handling of family allowance cheques we may get some information. It is

true that over a period of time we are going to find the number of cheques that will be handled will perhaps be doubled. I am sure that if the ordinary production line system were used it would not mean that we have to double the number of machines or the number of people who handle those machines. Perhaps 10 machines have been ordered with a certain capital expenditure. If ordinary production line methods are used I think the purchase of an additional two machines and perhaps an increase of 25 per cent in the labour force would produce twice the results. This is the lesson that can be learned from watching industry in action, and it is a lesson that there seems to be no reason to believe could not be applied to government.
Sometimes we ask ourselves, how do these terrific costs arise? In connection with the expenditure of our money on the armed forces, I find that for the current fiscal year approximately 43-9 per cent of the defence dollar is going to be spent on the air force. It is a very worthy branch of the service on which to spend it. We are talking about a lot of money because during the year we will spend on the armed services altogether approximately $1,863 million.
I would refer to the article concerning the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) appearing in the latest issue of Canadian Business. Approximately 43 per cent of this money will be spent on the air force. Someone may say, "I wonder how they can waste any money there." Well, the Globe and Mail of May 2 contained an article dealing with the answer to a question tabled in the house. It was shown that there were 5,570 air crew applicants for the air force during the year, and that 4,000 of them were rejected. Obviously if this type of recruiting program, whatever it may be, continues, then it can be expected that to recruit 1,570 men it is going to cost many times the amount that should be set aside for that purpose.
These are the things we should look into if we are going to save money-publication costs, and items of that kind. As I said before, I wish to stay clear of other items to which reference has been made from time to time-and I am referring to the payments of various grants through the welfare branches of government.
I could give another illustration, because I have in my hand another of these divorce bills from the other place, the only difference being that this time it would seem that they are going to put them on nice, sugar-coated stock. It is much nicer, and fills more paper. I am sure it does not perform any better service, and that it continues to find its way into the wastepaper baskets of all members.

These are places where we should look for economy. We could expect economies if an independent commission were set up to take a real look at the situation. I listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) speak about the duties in the house, and the committees to which various items might be referred. Surely after the performance we have had at this session, a performance which at every turn has refused us the information we require, we cannot expect to get economies or to get at the basis for economies in the various government departments through the utilization of that method. As a matter of fact, if that is the type of scrutiny that is to be allowed, then all I can say is that most of us will rot in our places before we will get the information we need.
